This might be a good time for the Minister of Transport-he is leaving the house; if we could get him back in-
Why?

It would be a good opportunity for the Minister of Transport to deal with the matter I raised on orders of the day rather than leave it to Monday evening, when he is allowed by the rules of the house only about three minutes in which to

explain what is happening at Toronto international airport.
The Globe and Mail of this morning states that some four drivers who participated in a demonstration protesting against a monopoly which has been granted to Air Terminal Transport Limited to solicit passengers at the airport have been fined, and that the R.C.M.P. at the airport have taken the names of more than 100 drivers who have picked up fares there. This is not a matter of earth shaking importance and I do not wish to delay the committee, but it seems to me that some statement should be forthcoming from the minister. I do not think the practice followed at Malton is the practice at other airports; if it is, it certainly ought to be reviewed. Why should we grant one company a monopoly to solicit passengers at an airport while all other taxi drivers are not only barred but, as can be seen from this report, are actually arrested-
Arrested?
-and fined for soliciting passengers at the airport.

Have they been taken
into custody?

No. I assume they were picked up by the police, that their names were taken and that they appeared before the courts. But these four who were fined would appear to be only the vanguard of a much larger number. If the report is correct, the R.C.M.P. have taken the names of a hundred other taxi drivers who participated in this demonstration and were soliciting customers.
I think the minister should indicate whether it is his intention to discontinue this monopoly. It seems to me it is contrary to the general practice that a building erected from public funds, or rather the traffic generated by such a building, should be made the exclusive monopoly of one company and that other persons in the business of transporting the general public should be denied the opportunity to solicit passengers there. It is true that other taxi drivers can bring passengers to the airport and unload them, but they are not allowed to pick them up; and the reports in this morning's newspapers indicate that some 500 taxi drivers have stated their intention of defying this rule next week and challenging the validity of this franchise by actually picking up fares at the airport. If this happens the minister will be kept busy prosecuting taxi drivers. In the circumstances I think the committee should be given some explanation by the minister.

I am very happy to give an explanation. If I seemed discourteous to the hon. gentleman I certainly did not intend to be, but the situation is far too complicated to be answered in the naive fashion in which the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm seems to think all questions can be answered.
It is apparent that a monopoly in this situation, especially a private monopoly, is distasteful to most of us, and I do not blame anyone for expressing a reaction similar to that which has been expressed today by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. But there are certain circumstances which should be considered.
In the first place, let me say this is the practice not only in Toronto but at all the major airports of Canada. The reason it exists-and it has been going on for years; there is nothing new about it-is to ensure that there will be an adequate supply of taxis available to carry passengers who wish to use them throughout the whole of the period when aircraft are using the airport. In return for this monopoly the company has to pay a percentage of its take to the government. In other words the taxpayers do get reimbursed by the company-and they are not too badly reimbursed, either, I may say-in return for granting this exclusive privilege. So the exclusive privilege is not a free gift to the company; it is a right for which rent is paid to the taxpayers.
After representations had been made to me by most of the members from Toronto some two or three weeks ago, I asked the head of this company to come to see me here in Ottawa. I questioned him about some of the allegations of public dissatisfaction which had been made here in the house and which had come to my attention through the press. I suggested to him that there were taxis which went out to the airport, and naturally they did not want to go back empty; they wished, if they could, to pick up fares.
One does not blame the drivers for that. That is how they earn their living. I had had some correspondence with the metropolitan Toronto taxi council-I think that is the name of the organization; I am speaking from memory-and I said "Why not make an offer to these people, or let them make an offer to you, to have a certain number of places made available to them in return for which they can contribute in exactly the same way you do, so they would have a chance to pick up fares before going back"? I added that it would not be expected that they would get this privilege free, but we would not impose
Interim Supply
conditions on them, as we do on you, to have cars available 24 hours a day. I stated that if they could make an amicable arrangement among themselves which was fair both to the taxpayers and to the users of the service so that this grievance would be ended I could assure them that the Department of Transport would approve. I might add that in my assessment of the priorities, both the taxpayers and the air passengers deserve to be considered before either of these carriers.
The head of the company which has the monopoly told me he had never been approached by this taxi council. That did not surprise me particularly. I wrote to the council myself and suggested they approach the company to see if they could not work out some amicable arrangement of the kind I am suggesting, and indicated that I would be very happy if some such agreement could be reached. But as far as I am able to learn there is only one taxi company, not the whole council, engaged in this particular demonstration at the moment, and certain of the activities of this company-I do not wish to go into it now, though I could at some time when there is greater opportunity-suggest to me that perhaps it does not reflect a very large popular feeling, but mainly a desire on its part to skim a little of the cream off this traffic without assuming any responsibilities whatever.
I would say, in summary, that I believe the passengers who travel by air to great airports such as Malton are entitled, as far as it can be arranged, to have a taxi service available to them when they arrive; that this cannot be done on a hit or miss basis by simply allowing the kind of undiluted free enterprise that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam is such a strong advocate of; that there has to be some measure of organization and regulation to ensure that on the whole-though there are some genuine grievances about this matter, and I think any person providing a monopoly service must be watched very carefully all the time, no matter who he is- an adequate service is provided. I think the only practical way of assuring sufficient transport at the hours of the day when there is not much business is to give to the people who provide that service an assurance that they will get such traffic as is offered. That is the problem.
I do not think we are going to have mass arrests at all. At the present time I am told this particular company has a number of taxis that just keep driving at a slow pace around the airport, which is quite contrary to the law; they are simply trying to take the law

Interim Supply
into their own hands. I do not think anyone in the house would argue that this should be tolerated for any length of time; but one does not like to see the drivers of the cars penalized because of the policy of the head of the company.
I am giving very careful consideration to the most effective way of dealing with this problem, but I do believe the suggestion I made, that the taxi council should get in touch with this company that has the monopoly and see if they can work out some arrangement along the lines I suggested, is the most practical way. If, however, a more practical method could be suggested, I am not wedded to the particular system that is there now. But I think everybody who has had much experience of travelling does know that the ordinary traveller arriving at Malton is able to get a cab without much delay, and that the rates are substantially the same as those charged by other similar public carriers. I think this is the prime consideration, and it must be kept in the front of our minds while we endeavour to settle this matter as justly and as fairly as possible.

Mr. Chairman, in regard to the minister's description of me as being in favour of undiluted free enterprise, I am even more opposed to private monopolies, particularly when these private monopolies are selected by a government on some basis which has never been explained; that is, why a particular company is selected and given a concession to operate a monopoly in transporting people from airports. This concession may have been given to them by tender publicly called for, with regard to which other companies had an opportunity to bid and a chance to rent the concession. If that is true, of course there can be less objection to it.
However, Mr. Chairman, I want to make just two points to the minister. The first is that the newspaper reports on this matter- and this is the only information I have-would seem to indicate that this question involves more than one company. The statement in this morning's paper would seem to indicate that almost the entire Toronto taxi council, I think it is called, are incensed about this monopoly and the fact that their members have been denied the right to solicit fares at the airport.
I wanted to ask the minister at how many airports across Canada this policy is followed. If I recall correctly, I have been at airports at which a number of different taxis were picking up fares. I agree with the minister that there has to be some orderly arrangement in this matter. There is little value in having
[Mr. PickersgiH.1
100 taxis at the airport at one hour and no taxis at all at another hour; there has to be some orderly arrangement-so that people arriving at the airport at very unusual hours can be sure there will be transportation available. This is particular true in the early hours of the morning: people do not want to wait while they phone for a taxi, particularly when the airport is as far out from the centre of the city as is the Malton airport. I can understand the minister has to have some arrangement that will serve the passengers to the best possible advantage.
I would like to ask the minister if this is a general policy which he intends to follow, and whether it is not possible to work out some arrangement by which a number of companies could rent parking places, with the understanding that they would pay a rent; that they would have taxis there at all times, or at certain specified times, to pick up passengers so this business could be spread around rather than appearing to place what constitutes a private monopoly solely in the hands of one firm. While the minister is answering, Mr. Chairman, he might also tell me whether this concession was given to this company and to other companies in other places on the basis of public tender.

Mr. Chairman, I will first of all deal with the first question, as to whether this is a general policy. I cannot say for sure just how many airports are involved in this practice. It applies in Ottawa, I know; it applies in Montreal, I know; it applies in St. John's, Newfoundland; it even applies at Gander, and I would think it applied in Winnipeg, Edmonton and Vancouver. I do not really know where else it would apply, but I do think it has been almost universal at airports where there is any considerable traffic.
With regard to the company that now has the monopoly in Toronto, I was not the minister concerned with this matter, and the present government was not in office when the contract was made. By saying that I am not imputing any blame to anybody at all; all I am saying is that the present company was given this contract three or four years ago-I think, four. I do not believe there were public tenders called, but there are some difficulties about calling public tenders because the only people who can operate this kind of service are those who are properly licensed under another authority than ours. That is to say, we do not have the right and this parliament does not have the jurisdiction, as I understand it, to license taxi companies

and companies of that sort unless perchance they are in interprovincial service, and none of these are. Therefore any competition there might be would have to be limited to those people who are unable to get a provincial, or in some cases perhaps a municipal licence. That is just another of the complications.
Whether it would be possible to divide this business up, I am not quite sure. I am told that most taxi companies would not find it very attractive if they had to meet the conditions that apply. No doubt some of them would like to come in on this business-particularly this Yellow Cab company-when it suits them and when they know there are going to be enough passengers to pick up at the airport. After all, I have made a suggestion to the metropolitan council which, it seems to me, is exactly along the line suggested by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. I believe that the right way for these people to act is in a lawful manner, instead of attempting to flout the law, which I do not think any government can be expected to condone.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I could ask the Minister of Transport a couple of questions concerning this matter. As I understand it the minister has suggested a private arrangement whereby these people would work this matter out for themselves. In view of the ten year contract which was granted in 1960, I think this might be an acceptable solution. I suggest that Air Terminal Transport, which has the monopoly, should be required to give the service, perhaps in return for allowing other taxicabs to pick up there although perhaps not 24 hours a day. They have a starter there and they could extract a fee for every pick-up made by another cab company. Perhaps that sort of arrangement would work. However, I did not quite understand the minister's suggestion, and I do not know whether that is what he had in mind; perhaps he could confirm it.
The other question I wanted to ask concerns the service which is given. Has the minister anything to add on the question of providing service to the whole of metropolitan Toronto, not just a bus service from Toronto international airport to the Royal York hotel? It is my view, and I certainly find general acceptance of this view, that metropolitan Toronto is a very large municipality indeed, and merely obtaining bus service to the Royal York hotel does not really help me or my constituents one iota. No service at all is given to the 350,000 people who live in the northern and eastern parts of
Interim Supply
Toronto. I am sure the same thing applies to people who live at the other extremity, although they are much closer to the airport and do not run into the same sort of cab fare.
I should like to ask the minister whether there has been any further development concerning this matter with Air Terminal Transport and whether they will offer any service particularly to the northern and eastern parts of Toronto. I might say right now that I am not prepared to accept the excuse that the construction presently under way on highway 401 would prevent such a service from being implemented. We all know that highway 401 is very crowded. Nevertheless, in spite of the construction, the department of highways of the Ontario government has continuously maintained four paved lanes during the construction, so I do not think this is sufficient reason for not giving us this sort of service. If Air Terminal Transport take the position that they will not give bus service to the northern and eastern parts of Toronto until highway 401 is completed, then I think the discussion is somewhat academic because their contract would undoubtedly expire before the construction is completed in 1970. I wonder whether the minister would have anything to say about that.

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. gentleman has anticipated most of what I would have to say on this subject. I did talk to the company about giving service to an area with a population at least as great as that of the city of Hamilton, which has such a service, and they said they were contemplating doing that as soon as highway 401 was reasonably passable. Not having travelled on highway 401 recently I was not able from personal experience to refute this argument. However, I did mention it to the hon. member and to certain other hon. members who, although they are not political supporters of the Ontario government, in this particular matter seemed to defend the Ontario department of highways by suggesting that highway 401 is perfectly passable even though once in a while it was rather congested with traffic, like a lot of other roads.
I intend to make further representations to the company on this particular point, and I also thought I would suggest to them that the first time I was in Toronto they might drive me over highway 401 in one of their cars and let me judge for myself whether the highway was hopelessly congested. Perhaps I can also arrange for one or two other members who might be going to Toronto to have

Interim Supply
that experience themselves. I think the company is aware of the fact that practically all the members from metropolitan Toronto, from whatever part of the house, feel rather keenly about this matter, and the company is in a frame of mind where they would be anxious to do anything which would seem reasonable.
I might say to the minister that they have no objection to travelling on highway 401 for $9.75 a trip.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think we should try to proceed in an orderly fashion. This is developing into a debate between two members. I think everyone should be given the chance to participate in the debate at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I want to ask the minister a question or two in regard to this general problem. The discussion so far has been limited to airports; at least what I have heard of it has been. Does not this same principle apply to railway stations, or to certain railway stations, in Canada? I do not know whether it applies to railway stations operated by the railway companies themselves, but I think it does apply to some railway stations which are operated by terminal companies.
While the minister is looking into this question with regard to airports perhaps he would also inform the house what is the jurisdiction, if any, and the supervision, if any, of the Department of Transport with regard to monopolies of this sort which operate at railway stations. I have had the experience at certain railway stations where a cab would drive up and unload passengers, and then when I proceeded to ask the cab to take me somewhere I was curtly told that the driver could not pick up passengers at that point. I have been told to get out of the cab and take a taxi belonging to the right company in order to go to my destination.

Mr. Chairman, I think I can deal with that matter very quickly. The government has no jurisdiction in this field. We do not operate any railway stations, and the cabs would be under provincial jurisdiction.

Perhaps the minister might make available to the members of the committee some of the services these contracting companies are required to provide. I do not mean what they are paid in terms of dollars and cents, but the services they are required

to provide at each airport. That might give us a better understanding of the problem.

I would be very happy to make those documents available. I think the simplest thing would be to table them, and I will try to do that on Monday; or in view of a certain engagement I have, if I did it on Tuesday perhaps I would be forgiven.

Mr. Chairman, I might point out for the information of hon. members that we in Edmonton are now back to the happy situation, we think, of one standard contractor in this respect. For a number of years there was always a problem with dual contractors, either once a week or once a month. The minister can consult his files, but I am sure he knows that Edmonton international airport may be engraved on the hearts of certain officials of his department as a result of certain concessions which were made. When they die I am sure it will be engraved on their hearts, because it gave them nothing but trouble.
I would point out to hon. members that the conditions of these contracts are very stringent. The department does get a substantial return, which is part compensation for the facilities which are provided at international airports by the crown of Canada. In addition to that, are the so-called non-privileged taxi companies prepared to put up the equivalent of automobile insurance for the protection of passengers, as is required of the contractor under his contract with the crown? Are the drivers to be uniformed? Again, are they to be there at all hours? After all, a private individual in a taxi business for himself will go after the traffic wherever it is, whatever the hour of the day. Is the contractor going to make sure there are cars available during all hours of the night when there is little traffic and yet there is a requirement for taxis. All a passenger who is unable to obtain taxi service has to do is complain to the air line; then there follows a quick reaction on the part of the taxi contractor.
I can assure hon. members that this business of unlimited pick-up service at an international airport can lead to grief. I have heard of slashed tires and sugar cubes in gas tanks. Competition gets a little rugged at times. I am not suggesting the people involved in this dispute are resorting to that sort of thing, but it certainly has been the experience in many places that when you have this rather keen competition for passengers times do get rough. It is far better for the department, the air lines and the passengers to have the

facilities handled under one reputable contractor who, after all, originally got his contract on the basis of a tender.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with interest to the many remarks passed on the Toronto Malton airport during the past hour. I hope I will not be threshing old straw when I also refer to the situation, but as a member from metropolitan Toronto and one who uses the Malton airport considerably I would like to ask the Minister of Justice if he could not arrange to have the R.C.M.P. officer, who chases passengers from taxicab to taxicab, garbed in one of those brilliant red uniforms during the summer season, as I understand tourists get more enjoyment seeing red-coated Mounties chasing passengers from taxicab to taxicab than is the case when they have those buff coloured uniforms which they were wearing last Friday when I arrived and stepped into a Yellow cab.
This business of the airport has got to the position. I also congratulate him on the the Minister of Transport for returning to the chamber, as suggested by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam a few moments ago, and I admire him for his statement this morning that he is not wedded to this monopoly position. I also congratulate him on the statement he made some weeks ago in which he said he is an old time Liberal and does not believe in monopolies. I would ask him to put his beliefs and convictions on that score into effect in the immediate future.
The situation I want to draw to the committee's attention, and which has not been referred to this morning, is that some months ago the Toronto transit commission, which is a publicly owned municipal service in metropolitan Toronto, began to operate a bus out to Malton airport. It runs along Dixon road to the town of Weston and connections are made there throughout metropolitan Toronto.
There were a number of raised eyebrows in Toronto over the fact that the R.C.M.P., in either red coats or buff coloured coats, had not been sent down to get hold of Ralph Day, chairman of the Toronto transit commission, to advise him he was trespassing on a private monopoly of Air Terminal Transport, but there was some oversight so that they were not sent out after the Toronto transit commission in the way they are sent out after private taxis which pick up fares at the airport.
However, the Department of Transport apparently has another way of choking off competition for Air Terminal Transport, as this letter which I will read shows. This
Interim Supply
bus was run into the air terminal in order to pick up passengers seeking bus transfer into the metropolitan centre, and on Wednesday of this week I received a letter written by Mr. Clarence C. Downey, a former chairman of the Toronto transit commission and still a member of the commission, a former reeve of the village of Swansea and former warden of the county of York, a very experienced gentleman. He has written to me as follows:
As you probably know, I am an ex-chairman and am presently a commissioner with the Toronto transit commission. As such, I was greatly interested in our newspaper reports of the discussion initiated by you in parliament of the exclusive franchise for transportation at our international airport (Toronto) granted in 1960 to Air Terminal Transport Limited.
I became interested in this matter some months ago on visiting the airport when I saw one of our T.T.C. buses sitting outside the terminal proper-some one third of a mile from the actual entrance and with a very substantial incline up to such entrance from the bus.
I took up the matter with our officials and T.C.A. officials-we even had the bus driven into the airport proper to see if it could negotiate the turns and found it could do so.
I may say in passing that I had heard the bus could not make the turns in between the cement columns, but Mr. Clarence Downey points out that he proved it can be driven into the airport and negotiate these turns.
I was then hopeful that our public transportation vehicle, to serve the airport employees and the public generally, would be permitted to enter the terminal. After all this negotiation and demonstration, however, we were advised that due to the prior commitment our request could not at present be granted.
It seems to me ridiculous that public transportation should not be provided at a nationally owned airport for those employees and the public generally who cannot afford the fares which Air Terminal Transport charges and who also are not being served throughout the metropolitan area. This limited company cannot hope nor can it be expected to provide metro-wide services as can be provided by the T.T.C.
I feel that the exclusive, monopolistic transportation franchise granted to Air Terminal Transport Limited should not exclude public transportation services that the T.T.C. can provide.
I appreciate the fact that it might become a straight legal problem but I feel that sufficient pressure in parliament might induce Air Terminal Transport Limited to favourably consider allowing public transportation vehicles to provide a service which it cannot provide.
I would appreciate hearing from you.
Sincerely,
C. C. Downey,
Commissioner.
Now we have the interesting situation of a federally owned piece of property, the air terminal, having given an exclusive franchise

Interim Supply
to Air Terminal Transport Limited, a funeral coach limousine service, by which they are holding up the publicly owned Toronto transportation commission when it seeks to give service to the people using that public service, the air terminal.
Why should there be a toll gate between the federal government and the municipal government on this matter, and why should there be a toll gate between the Department of Transport and privately owned taxicab companies. A moment or two ago the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked whether the contract to provide transport service to the air terminal in Toronto had been put up for tender. I can assure him quite definitely that it was not put up for tender. I have in my hand a copy of a letter dated November 25, 1963, from the former minister of transport to Mr. Vernon Singer, M.P.P. of Toronto, in which the third last paragraph reads:
When the agreement with Air Terminal Transport Limited was up for renewal in 1960, a tender call was considered but it was not possible to proceed on this basis because of the position taken by the provincial department of transport in respect to franchises.
I make the statement in this house without any fear of successful contradiction that that statement is absolutely false, even though it appears in a letter written on government stationery. If the federal government, through the Department of Transport, should grant a franchise to any company to operate a passenger conveyance service out of the Mal-ton airport, you can rest assured that the Ontario department of transport would issue the necessary permit. I have taken that matter up with officials of the Ontario government and have been assured that if such a contract were negotiated there would be no hold-up provincially.
This is a specious argument advanced by whoever wrote that letter. I am certain that the minister who signed the letter did not write it. There are so many fallacies in it that it would be a disgrace to put it on the record, but that is the answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam.
I have protested in the house before, and on this motion for interim supply I wish to protest again against the federal government signing an indenture for a passenger conveyance service which nine times in seven pages refers to a taxi station, taxi service, taxi operation, taxi this, taxi that; yet the company with which they have the agreement does not have a taxi licence. How in

the name of heaven can you make an agreement with a steam railroad unless you are dealing with a steam railroad? You do not sign a contract with electric radial cars and specify what the steam railroad service is to be once the contract is signed.
Here we have an agreement signed by the hon. member for Three Rivers, the former minister of transport, in 1961 granting Air Terminal Transport Limited a taxi service. Yet Air Terminal Transport Limited does not operate a single taxi, has not got a taxi licence in the city of Toronto and has not got a taxi licence in the township of Toronto.
To me the agreement is palpably false because it calls for services that are not being rendered. The company is providing what I prefer to call a funeral coach service using long black Pontiacs, and this is supposed to add status to those people who are forced to travel economy class on T.C.A. because that is the only class of ticket made available to members of parliament.
In this letter of the Department of Transport dated November 25, 1963 the statement is made in several places that it is necessary that there be conveyances available at the airport when air travellers arrive. Why does the Department of Transport not show the same solicitude for people who arrive in Toronto by bus or people who arrive in Toronto by railway or people who arrive in Toronto by cars that break down at the city limits? No; it is only those persons travelling by air for whom the government appears to be extremely solicitous and for whom the government wants to make arrangements that there shall be transportation available at every moment.
In the letter to which 1 have referred the writer has this to say with regard to the situation in New York city:
At IdlewUd airport in New York the understanding of the situation there is that the former arrangement whereby taxicabs waited in a taxi rank and paid a fee of 25 cents per trip to the airport has been cancelled because it was found unworkable. The New York airport, by virtue of the tremendous numbers of passengers handled, does permit the free operation of taxis, provided they park in the designated taxi stand. But again, because of the nature of the New York operation, these taxis do not offer any serious competition to the air line bus service which operates point to point between the city terminal and the airport.
The Department of Transport admits that taxis are free to operate out of Idlewild airport in New York city, the biggest airport of its kind on the North American continent. Are we so special that we cannot follow the

example set by the biggest airport on the continent and give the same service to the public as air travellers enjoy in New York?
I have arrived at Idlewild airport in New York in the middle of a rainstorm and have had to wait 40 minutes before I could get any transportation downtown because every available vehicle was in operation. I have arrived at Logan airport in Boston at two o'clock in the morning and there was no public transportation available. My wife and I sat in the airport until a taxi came from the centre of Boston, picked us up and took us down to our hotel. I have arrived at Kansas City airport in the middle of the night, and as there was no taxi service available and no such service provided by the air lines I walked with other travellers from the airport. Hon. members may recall that the former airport used to be at the bow in the river and it was only a matter of eight or nine blocks for me to walk to the Muehlbach hotel.
There is no requirement that an airport must provide service at every hour of the day or night. In fact in this indenture, which as I have mentioned before I was unable to obtain from the previous government when I sat in opposition but which I received with ease from the former minister of transport, Mr. Mcllraith, last year, there is the following requirement:
-the lessee shall maintain at the said airport a sufficient number of buses, limousines and taxis, 24 hours each day, to accommodate passenger traffic to and from the said airport.
The president of the company told me to my face in the Seaway Towers hotel on the 15th of June that he does not operate any buses on Saturday or Sunday because there are not enough passengers travelling to and from the airport. But the agreement says he shall operate buses, limousines and taxis 24 hours each day. I have already shown that he does not operate taxis because he has not got a taxi licence. Here we have a requirement to operate a sufficient number of buses, limousines and taxis 24 hours each day, and I draw attention to the fact that he does not operate taxis, and he admits that on Saturdays and Sundays he does not operate buses. This is quite an agreement; yet people stand up and say it should be enforced.
With regard to the statement that has been made that only one taxi company seems concerned about this matter, I would point out that I have sat in on several meetings of the Toronto taxicab conference. The representatives or owners of a great majority of the taxicab companies in Toronto have attended
Interim Supply
these meetings, and we have discussed the contract between the Department of Transport and Air Terminal Transport Limited.
The complaint is not a specific one by one cab company. It is a complaint of all the taxicab operators in the city of Toronto.
I am happy to know that the Minister of Transport is on record in Hansard as having stated that when so many complaints reach his ears from Liberal and N.D.P. members from metropolitan Toronto about the taxicab service out of Malton airport, he realizes there is something wrong and that there must be grounds for complaint or all these members would not be complaining. As a matter of fact, two members of the cabinet from Toronto were in his office when protests were made to him about this unjust and unfair contract which prevents taxicabs from operating out of Malton airport.
A question was raised a while ago about the railway station contract. The union station advertises for tenders for cabs to make exclusive use of the lower level at the union station. The taxicab companies submit tenders and the successful bidder is given the exclusive right to operate taxicabs at the lower level of the union station where the government owned railway and the C.P.R. disembark passengers. The interesting thing about the situation at the union station is that taxicabs are free to pick up all the passengers they wish at any other entrance to the union station. The situation in Toronto is only exclusive in so far as the lower level is concerned, and this does not apply to the entire station. Why there should be an arrangement at Malton airport whereby the company providing limousine service is given exclusive rights over the whole area is beyond my comprehension.
In this morning's Globe and Mail, to which much reference has been made, there is a story about four taxicab operators being fined at Brampton and four being acquitted. I was talking to some of them on the long distance telephone yesterday, but rather than raise questions about the matter yesterday I thought I would speak on interim supply today. However, questions were asked in advance of my remarks. The interesting thing about the story in the Globe and Mail is that here we have a three column headline "Taxis Plan Airport Fight As Four Fined, Four Acquitted". We are told that Malton airport is public property and since the Minister of Transport has entered into a private contract that private contract is enforceable. It

Interim Supply
is private ground, because the Department of Transport has control over it.
Immediately below the story about the taxi operators there is a story about the action of a magistrate in Oakville, Ontario, approximately 20 miles from Brampton. Magistrate Kenneth Langdon freed a youth by the name of Terrance Page who had been accused of trespassing on a shopping centre in Oakville. The magistrate freed the boy on the charge of trespassing on a shopping centre and the story reads in part as follows:
Magistrate Langdon said the petty trespass act was enacted to keep persons from unlawfully trespassing on private property but in the case of commercial places there was an invitation to the public from the stores in the plaza to visit them. The magistrate said the key word in the act was "unlawful", which meant that an offence against the law had to be involved.
I would point out that there are a large number of stores at Malton airport which are seeking public patronage. There are gift shops, newsstands and the like. In their way they constitute a small shopping plaza. Yet on the front page of the Globe and Mail we see that four taxi operators have been fined for parking on property owned by the Department of Transport, while at the same time a magistrate at Oakville in another case says you cannot prosecute a boy for moving about on a privately owned shopping plaza because it is public in every aspect. This is a very interesting conflict of opinion between two magistrates.
I should like to make it a matter of public record that the taxicab operators who were fined in Brampton yesterday speak very highly and very kindly of the magistrate. They said he gave them every possible consideration. They are planning to appeal. They have no feeling against Magistrate Ord, I believe it was, in Brampton.
It was quite interesting to find right below this taxi statement that Magistrate Langdon said you could not be arrested for trespassing on a shopping plaza. If you cannot be arrested for trespassing on a shopping plaza, how can you be arrested for trespassing on Department of Transport property? We do not advertise for tenders for a taxi service here at the parliament buildings. If it is a good thing to let a contract for taxi service at Malton airport and make some money out of it, why is it not a good thing to do the same thing for the parliament buildings? If they say it is highly important to have taxis available at the airport, they could say with equal force that it is highly important to have taxis available 
for members of parliament and visitors at the parliament buildings. It is ridiculous.
I regret spending so much time on Malton when the subject was discussed during the question period, and when such a frank statement was made on the subject by the Minister of Transport. If I have any time left, and if I have not I shall deal with it on another occasion, I should like to make some reference to the statement made by the Minister of Transport a week ago last Wednesday regarding CATV operations in this country. I want to state that as a member of this house and as a Canadian taxpayer, as well as one who believes he knows a little bit more than zero about television and the radio industry, that there is no need for these statements being issued. I really believe there will be a long drawn out controversy over this situation.
On July 22, about a week ago, the Minister of Transport rose in the house and made a statement with regard to a proposed order concerning ownership of CATV operations. Then there was a proposal concerning an item re CATV receiving stations being included in the supplementary estimates. This proposal re CATV receiving stations being dealt with by an item in the supplementary estimates is something that is going to irritate Canadians as a whole when they learn the facts.
CATV is something that is absolutely unknown to the vast majority of Canadians because there is no necessity for such an installation in their areas. However, this does not get around the fact that there are approximately 340 companies holding CATV licences from the Department of Transport. They are quite happy to deal with the Department of Transport. They do not want to be removed from the wings of the Department of Transport. If you now bring the board of broadcast governors into the picture, they of course will impose a form of censorship.
I am using the word "censorship" by choice and as a result of experience in the situation.
Under this proposed item re CATV receiving stations being brought under the board of broadcast governors, you are going to' have the ridiculous situation of the federal government through the board of broadcast governors enforcing censorship over a minority of the people. These approximately 340 licensed CATV companies service about 300,000 viewers in Canada. It is estimated that 5 per cent of the total television viewers in the dominion now have CATV. There are

three types of CATV operation to which I should like to draw your attention.
Apartment house owners put up a CATV system by erecting a high tower on the apartment. Depending on the number of tenants, anywhere from say 40 up to 800 apartment house dwellers will use this service. You have a CATV operation because with one high tower they can get a much better picture for the tenants than if everyone had rabbit ears hanging out the windows. The owners of apartment houses would not want to have rabbit ears sticking out of every apartment house window. The tenants pay an extra charge per month for this television service. There is no complaint because the picture comes in very clearly.
The second type of CATV operation covers real estate subdivisions where, in this day and age of affluence under a Liberal government, we find more posh suburban areas being developed by real estate operators. It seems the public do not want telephone wires or hydro wires hanging in the air or even television antennas. Arrangements are made, therefore, to bury the wire services within the real estate development and underground go the television services and all the rest of them. The picture is received by a tall antenna which does not disfigure the neighbourhood. The picture is received very clearly. The people who buy this service enter into a contract to pay for it.
The third type of CATV, which I have mentioned in this house before and of which I give you a direct example, involves the place near which my summer home is located; Penetang, north of Toronto. If you do not have CATV the only thing you can pick up is the Barrie television station. I have nothing against the Barrie television station personally, and I do not have CATV because I am 11 miles out of Penetang. However, I know many people in the area who are willing to pay for the extra service of CATV in order that they can pick up other programs than the ones that come in from Barrie. They want a choice of programs, and they are willing to pay for that service.
This proposal to put CATV receiving stations ultimately under the board of broadcast governors will not affect the CATV operations in apartment houses. We have the assurance of the minister that he has no intention of having apartment house CATV interfered with in this way. It will not affect CATV operations in real estate subdivisions. It will only affect that one third of CATV installations about which I have been speaking lat-
Interim Supply
terly, and will therefore affect much less than 5 per cent of the television viewers.
If the board of broadcast governors is going to adopt the attitude it has taken in the past- and there is no reason for expecting it to change-it will be telling the applicants for CATV installations that they are going to interfere with the successful operation of some neighbouring television station. This would be a terrible thing, to let free enterprise find its level in this country of ours. The board of broadcast governors claim they must see that television stations have an economically successful life. CATV opposition will mean people will be looking at CATV programs and not looking at a local or nearby television station.
I say it is absolutely not the function of the government to make certain that every television or radio station is able to make a profit. Either we believe in free enterprise or we do not believe in free enterprise. We are not going to impose censorship on about 1 per cent of the television viewers of Canada by intimating that a CATV application by people who wish to get around the local television station shall be dealt with by the board of broadcast governors, when a CATV installation is not opposed for apartment house dwellers and when a CATV installation in a real estate subdivision is not opposed.
In so far as the 95 per cent of Canadians who do not need CATV are concerned, they can pick up any station they want. In Toronto we can pick up Buffalo; we can pick up Hamilton, Toronto and some people can pick up Kitchener. If you happen to be fortunate enough to be in an area where you can make a choice between six or seven television stations, the board of broadcast governors will not interfere with your reception. If you live in a part of Canada in which there is only one local television station available and where CATV will bring you improved service, then the board of broadcasting governors is going to be asked to step in and say whether or not that CATV service will be made available to you.

I wonder if I could ask the hon. member for York-Humber if he would allow me to interrupt him for just a minute to make an apology to him and to the committee. I have a very urgent and long standing engagement at twelve o'clock. The president of the council is my acting minister when I am not available in the house. He has perforce to stay here anyway, and I am sure he will report anything that is said to me. I do not think at this stage I could add anything to

Interim Supply
what I have already said about the taxi situation, and I do not think I would wish to embark upon a debate at this time on CATV. Perhaps the committee and the hon. member would excuse me. But I wished to explain that I was not walking out on him.

I have already thanked the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate for returning to the house, and I am ready to repeat those thanks if he did not hear me the first time. I will conclude my remarks by stating it is unfair-

Would the hon. member mind replying to a question before the minister does leave? We are all interested in the representations he is putting forward, but did not he and his colleagues who share those views put them before the minister before he made this announcement?

I am willing to answer questions, but since the minister is here, maybe he might do so. I hear a certain amount of laughter. Might I answer that question then, by asking why do you think I am speaking in the House of Commons today?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka.

I notice, Mr. Chairman, that one or two hon. members have risen in connection with this subject and I would be quite happy to defer to the hon. member for Greenwood and the hon. member for Fraser Valley if they would like to continue along these lines. I believe my hon. friend from Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm would also like to speak.

I do not intend to unduly prolong the debate on this matter of the air terminal at Toronto. I see the minister has left. But I do wish to thank the minister for keeping in touch with me, as one of the Toronto members, in regard to this problem and letting me see the correspondence he has had with the taxicab people and with Air Terminal Transport Company.
I suggest to the minister that he look very carefully, if he has not done so, into the legal validity of this monopoly. He might also look carefully into the question raised by the hon. member for York-Humber, namely whether this monopoly has lived up to the terms of its own agreement. If it is not providing the services called for it certainly should not retain the benefits of the monopoly granted to it. I should like whoever is keeping in touch with the minister on this subject, now

that the minister has left, to convey those two suggestions to him as forcefully as he can.
If the commitments undertaken by the company have not been fully honoured, pressure could be brought to bear upon Air Terminal Transport Company to modify its monopoly position with a much greater chance of success than the mere making of a statement that it would be very nice if the company would consider writing to the taxicab conference making suggestions for changes. I think the minister would then be in a strong position to say to the transport company which has the monopoly, "We do not think you are living up to your end of the agreement and we insist on your modifying its terms."
I would point out that this is a matter of great importance to the many hundreds, indeed thousands of cab drivers whose livelihood is concerned, and also that the situation affects the convenience of a vast number of travellers. I think the hon. member for York-Scarborough is perfectly correct in his statement that there is no excuse in the world for not providing service to the east end of Toronto based on the pretext that highway 401 is not passable at the present time. It is passable.
They do it for $9.75 all the time.
I hope the minister will not allow this excuse to be used as a reason for not giving an adequate service to the people who live in Toronto east.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: I undertake to take note of the hon. member's comments and pass them on to the minister.

It had not been my intention to take part in the debate on interim supply, but in view of the fact that the discussion has proceeded for a considerable length of time I intend to beg the indulgence of the committee and discuss a few matters this afternoon.
Some questions have been raised with respect to the length of the debate. I maintain that the pattern as far as interim supply is concerned has been radically changed. It used to be that interim supply would go through in a few minutes or half an hour or half a day. But when the Liberal party was in opposition the pattern was changed and interim supply was debated for days at a time. Now there has been a change in government; we find the Liberals on the government side and the Conservatives are in opposition, and the

official opposition is taking the position that what the Liberals could do they can do better, and they are proceeding on that basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member would answer a question at this point. I am not sure whether he was in the house at the time, but he may recall that the occasion to which he referred, when the Liberals were in opposition and consideration of interim supply took longer than usual, was the time the government of that day was asking for eleven twelfths of supply with the estimates of no more than two departments opened after almost a year of continuous sitting.
And refusal to deliver a budget.

The hon. lady has asked whether I remember that particular situation. We do remember that the government was asking for interim supply month by month, and I think the circumstances today are somewhat comparable. Estimates were not brought in back in those days, and estimates are not being brought in at this particular session. I do not think we can make a clear distinction between the two situations. I still say the Conservatives are just paying the Liberals back in their own kind. They know it worked in those days; the government was upset, and no doubt they are hoping that history will repeat itself and that they will be able to upset the government.
However, I do not wish to spend any further time on that matter. I want to call attention to a situation having to do with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I was speaking to the Secretary of State the other evening and indicated it was my intention to raise some questions concerning the C.B.C. yesterday or today. He advised me that because of prior commitments he would not be able to be present in the committee. However, he knows we will be discussing these matters, and they will be brought to his attention.
We think of the C.B.C. as a publicly owned corporation. It is one which has come under serious fire on many occasions, mainly because those in charge have acted as though it were nobody's business how the corporation is operated, how the taxpayers' money is spent, what kind of programs are shown, or what actually are the policies governing its conduct. We remember, of course, that because of public pressure certain changes were made in programming some time ago and, of course, we give the C.B.C. full credit for acceding to the demands made on those occasions. But
Interim Supply
I believe the attitude which is taken by this publicly owned corporation is highly improper in view of the fact that this agency was established in order to assist the development of a distinctive Canadian culture, and in view of the fact that it is being maintained by funds provided by the taxpayers of this country.
The usual reply of the government to questions about the C.B.C. is that the government does not interfere with the operation of the corporation, and it would be improper for the government to apply any pressure on or endeavour to influence the C.B.C. in any way. I suppose that is basically true, and serious objection would no doubt be taken if the government itself interfered with the operations of this agency. Nevertheless we have to remember that the C.B.C. is responsible to parliament. Unless the C.B.C. recognizes that fact and is willing to conduct its affairs accordingly, then I think some serious consideration will have to be given to the whole matter of the C.B.C. and its operation and activities.
The request has been made many times for a parliamentary committee on broadcasting to be set up to give parliament an opportunity of calling witnesses and examining evidence. But, while the Secretary of State advises us that the C.B.C. is responsible to parliament, he blocks the way by refusing or neglecting to set up a body which could call for an accounting C.B.C. activities. Mr. Chairman, I would just call attention to the question that was asked by the hon. member for Cariboo just a short time ago, to which we have not yet received an answer. He asked if it was the intention of the minister to set up this particular body so that the C.B.C. could be called to account for its stewardship, but up to the present there has not been any reply to that question.
The minister announced, of course, that a committee was being set up, and no doubt has been set up, to go into the question of the C.B.C. and broadcasting activities in general. But may I suggest that this is no substitute for a parliamentary committee. It is true that it will go into all the different problems involved in the operation of this organization and broadcasting in general. No doubt it will study the whole matter from an academic point of view. But this will not take place of a committee of this house that can call for an account, dig into the details and demand answers, and find out just where we are going with regard to the operation of this publicly owned institution.

Interim Supply
I had the opportunity of directing a question to the Secretary of State just a few days ago. It had to do with a particular project in which the C.B.C. is co-operating. I refer to the Couchiching conference. Some days ago, or perhaps several weeks ago, we received a copy of the brochure that was put out by this particular organization, the Canadian institute on public affairs. Right on the front of the brochure it states that the conference this year is being conducted in co-operation with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The subject of this particular study was supposed to be "Order and good government". As I pointed out just a few days ago, there are several representatives from the Progressive Conservative party, several from the New Democratic party and several from the Liberal party at this conference, but for some strange reason or other they completely bypassed the Social Credit movement.
I raised the question-and I raise it again today-how is it that an agency purporting to institute a real study of the problems facing parliamentary government today bypassed an organization that since 1935 has been operating in the Dominion of Canada? Since 1935 they have formed the government in the province of Alberta; since 1952 they have formed the administration in the province of British Columbia; just a short time ago-in 1962, I believe-almost a million Canadians voted in support of Social Credit candidates. I say, Mr. Chairman, that for some strange reason or other this organization saw fit to bypass the Social Credit movement, and then tried to indicate that it was going to make an unbiased study of the problems that face parliamentary administration and parliament today.
The reason for this is the censure we have been under as the House of Commons, the problems we are facing now with our rules and our endeavour to change the rules to bring this institution up to date in its operations. I say that it can hardly give a rounded-out picture of opinion in this particular field when for some reason or other they ignore the existence of a political movement that has played an important part in the development of this country down through the last 30 years or so.
Mr. Chairman, I would call attention to the question I raised on July 10 in this particular connection. In reply the Secretary of State stated:
As far as X am aware the C.B.C. has no direct responsibility for selecting guest speakers at these

meetings. But in case the C.B.C. had something to do with it I will inquire, and report to the management the grievance of the hon. member.
Later on we were advised that this was a true statement, and the C.B.C. did not have anything to do with the appointment of speakers. This is what the minister stated, but I would call attention to the fact that apparently it is hardly accurate. I would like to refer to a remark which Mr. Reeves Haggan of the C.B.C. made to CTV news when this matter was under discussion. He said:
We didn't choose our participants on the basis of political parties.
Just where do we go from here, Mr. Chairman? The minister said the C.B.C. did not have anything to do with the appointment of speakers, and here Mr. Reeves Haggan of the C.B.C. stated that they did not choose their participants on the basis of political parties. I think we ought to get an answer to the question as to who is right and who is wrong. We ought to find out whether the C.B.C. did have anything to do with the selection of these speakers. I say, Mr. Chairman, that if the C.B.C. did have something to do with the selection of speakers, then they are to be censured because they did not insist on a completely rounded-out presentation of political opinion on these issues.
I would like to ask the question, why was the Social Credit movement discriminated against? They say "Oh, it was just an oversight. There was no discrimination at all". I would line to refer to another statement made by Mr. Reeves Haggan of the C.B.C. to CTV news. He stated:
It was the concensus of opinion that the people in the Social Credit party wouldn't contribute anything worth while to the conference.
Since when has the C.B.C. the right to set itself up as God in this country?
That is a good question.

I am just raising the question in relation to the C.B.C. I know that the Canadian institute on public affairs can do what it wants to do; it is a private organization, I suppose. But if it is working in cooperation with the C.B.C., and the C.B.C. is making a contribution and is having something to do with the operation of it, then I say that the C.B.C. has some answering to do.
We in this movement are not satisfied just to sit back and allow this kind of discrimination to continue. I have a comment here which was made over the CTV national news by Mr. Ab Douglas as to why Social Credit

was bypassed, ignored or discriminated against in the matter of the Couchiching conference. The comment is as follows:
That prestigious forum of public affairs known as the Couchiching conference will have to pull its head out of the sand if it is to continue to make a worth-while contribution to Canadian public life. "Order and good government" is the theme of this year's conference. Political speakers from various parts of the world have gathered on the shores of lake Couchiching, Ontario, to contemplate the problems facing parliamentary government in today's world. The rostrum of speakers is heavily weighted to the left. The Canadian institute of public affairs, the sponsoring organization, has invited a number of Canadian parliamentarians and politicians. Some from the ranks of the New Democrats, a few Liberals and Conservatives, but no representation from the Social Credit party.
Whether we or the eggheads at Couchiching like it or not, this party governs two of our biggest provinces and speaks for a large segment of the Canadian people in Ottawa. The Couchiching committee is being less than honest when it calls this snub an oversight. It was deliberate, based on the notion that small "1" liberalism is the only form of life the world of intellect can support. Without endorsing it, the right wing element is a fact of North American political life. In one way or another it contributes to parliamentary government in many countries. When the people at Couchiching return to the world of reality in a few days, they'll discover that you can ignore something you don't like, but it won't necessarily go away.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in trying to find the answer to why the Social Credit movement was completely ignored and bypassed in this matter, I should like to refer to a statement made by another analyst. This is a newspaper article by the hon. member for Port Arthur entitled "Definition makes room for thought". The hon. member referred to questions which I had raised in the House of Commons as to why Social Credit was being discriminated against in this particular matter, and went on to say:
He did not get an answer but it is easy to give one. The kind of persons who organize and attend Couchiching conferences do not take Social Credit seriously because neither its personalities nor its policies have any kind of intelligence or rational merit, as these people would see it. Thus the bill of politicians for this year includes New Democrats, Liberals and Conservatives. In each case, the politician invited has some reputation for either strong opinions or intellectual competence. Thus we will hear what Stanley Knowles and Pauline Jewett and Gordon Fairweather and George Nowlan have to say about parliamentary reform. Nothing from Bob Thompson and company.
Whether this is fair and just I'd hate to say.
I do not know why he would hate to say.
It is not representative. Without Social Crediters, even if they may be know-nothings and intellectual cretins, the conference hasn't all the facets of our parliamentary jewel.
I do not know where the hon. member obtained his right to pass supreme judgment
Interim Supply
on other people. He may be a self appointed judge; he may be a self styled intellectual. Nevertheless it all fits into the whole pattern, Mr. Chairman. Mr. Reeves Haggan of the C.B.C. gave the reasons. He said "We don't appoint them according to political parties". He also said it was the consensus of opinion that Social Credit would not be able to contribute anything.
I take this to be a direct insult to the people of the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia. Through the years since 1935 in the case of Alberta and since 1952 in the case of British Columbia the people there have seen fit to re-elect Social Credit administrations. If these eggheads or intellectuals, or whatever they want to call themselves, want to pass judgment on the electorate of Canada in that way, then I suppose we will have to let them go ahead and do it; but I want the people of those provinces to know what is being said.
My main reason for raising this matter today, Mr. Chairman, is to point out that here we have the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, a publicly owned institution, apparently deliberately discriminating against a sector of the Canadian people, and then purporting to present a full picture of the political views in this great nation of ours. Again I suggest that the taxpayers of the country may have to take another look at dishing out money and giving the C.B.C. a blank cheque if they cannot pull up their socks and begin to treat the people in the way they should be treated, instead of taking the position that they and they alone have the right to dictate what is put out over the air.
In conclusion let me once more call attention to the brochure entitled "Order and good government". On one of its pages appears these words:
It is being said that parliamentary government is in disrepute in Canada, its practitioners ill equipped, its procedures outmoded and the voters uninterested. Similar accusations can be read about the governments of Britain and the United States.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, although you will doubtless say I am biased, that it has been proven that in the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia there is good government. Perhaps there is in other provinces as well, but there certainly is in those provinces.
That is a matter of opinion.

Well, it is the opinion of the great majority of people there, as the hon. member very well knows. I cannot understand why these people try to downgrade

Interim Supply
their provinces all the time and criticize the provincial government's painting the picture as black as they can. I can understand this on the part of the members of the New Democratic party from the province of British Columbia because they almost made it there. They did not because the people repudiated them when Social Credit came along.
I have stated that I believe Social Credit can contribute something in this regard as far as good government is concerned. Therefore I believe there should be a recognition of this fact, and the C.B.C. should have seen to it that recognition was given to this matter. In fairness I should say that two days before the conference started I got an invitation to attend, which was rather short notice. I think the others had possibly several months' notice; I would not guarantee that, but I imagine they had.
For these reasons I think the C.B.C. had better take another look at the situation. If they expect parliament and members of parliament to continue to vote sums of money to support and carry on this work, then they are going to have to recognize the fact that they are responsible to parliament, and not appear to go along on their own hook and do whatever they want to do with the taxpayers' money.

I have only a few remarks to make, but in view of the serious charges brought by the hon. member against the C.B.C. and of the complaints made also by several members of the house, I feel that the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) should convince the government of the need to have the officers of this crown corporation appear before the appropriate committee so that we may ask them questions in the public interest.
I should like to deal now with the problem existing at present in certain Canadian airports with regard to the transportation of passengers, especially at the Dorval air terminal, where the Murray Hill Taxi Company holds an exclusive franchise for the conveyance of passengers. The executive committee of the city of Montreal, the taxi association and Montreal residents have spoken against the Dorval airport monopoly which goes against public interest.
In my opinion, the government should see what is being done in certain countries. Mr. Chairman, a person who lands at Beirut, Brasilia, Moscow and other capitals can take a taxi of his choice, contrary to what happens at Canada's main air terminals.

In view of the serious complaints made by the executive committee of the city of Montreal and the Montreal taxi association, I feel the government should change its policy entirely and accede to the wishes of Montreal residents.
Mr. Chairman, it is most important, since the world fair will be held in Montreal in 1967 and almost 50 million visitors.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

I would like to ask the hon.
member if he has a copy of the contract signed by the hon. member for Three Rivers, when he was minister, with the Murray Hill transportation people. In my case I had to get the contract from the former minister, the hon. member for Ottawa West. Have you a copy of the contract the hon. member for Three Rivers signed?

Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. member, I would say that I asked questions on the orders of the day some time ago in order to know what were the conditions of that concession, of that monopoly which was given to the Murray Hill Taxi Company by the Department of Transport. I did not get complete information and I must say that I shall ask soon further questions on the orders of the day so as to have all the necessary information in that respect.
I thank the hon. member for his question. [Text]
Why not ask Balcer?

I do not know; I have no idea. I will place another question on the order paper to get the full details on this. [Translation]
Since 50 million people from all over the world will be coming to Montreal in 1967 for the world fair, I feel it is important that after reaching agreements with the cities of Montreal and Dorval, the C.N.R. should build a monorail to carry travellers from the Dorval airport to Montreal.
I wonder if the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Cantin) has received a suggestion to that effect and if it is now under consideration.
I think that such a development would solve this problem of the transportation of travellers from the Dorval airport to Montreal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this government always appreciates every constructive suggestion. In the present case the hon. member is making his own the suggestions of the executive committee of the city of Montreal and of the Montreal taxi association as well as those made by members on this side of the house.
I have no doubt that following the comments made this morning by the Minister of Transport in connection with this matter, those suggestions will be studied and any possible improvement will be effected.
Mr. Chairman, I had asked for the floor earlier but was most encouraged to see that the debate on interim supply had taken a turn for the better, and I was pleased to see this.
Oh, oh.

If hon. members opposite will wait I will tell them why. Cabinet ministers and supporters of the government have been sitting in a somewhat non-communicative mood for the last four days and answered no questions whatever, although questions were raised on three separate departments and various other matters. The hon. members to my left, with only one or two exceptions, sat in stony silence for four days when very important subjects relating to the afEairs of Canada were raised.
I wonder is the hon. member referring to me.
No, I was not, Mr. Chairman.
I was just wondering to whom he was referring.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please.
I will answer the question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. As the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka has the floor, has the hon. member for Fraser Valley obtained permission from him to ask a question?
Could I get permission to ask a question?
I heard the question and I am prepared to answer.
Have you answered it?

I am waiting for you to sit down. The question I was asked by the hon. member for Fraser Valley was "Are you referring to me"? I was referring in general to all the other parties in the house except
Interim Supply
the Progressive Conservative opposition. I stated there were one or two members who did speak, but in general both the members on the government side and the members of the third, fourth and fifth parties sat in stony silence. This was the purport of my remarks, and I do not take them back.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I want to raise another subject which some of my colleagues will wish to pursue. We feel there is a department of government which should be discussed, and that is the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. As I say, I was very pleased to defer starting this particular debate because I thought that the pattern which was set today was an excellent one. There was a question raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam; there was a reply by the minister; there were various other remarks, and there were replies. In short, there was debate on the subject, and so I was most pleased to allow others to go ahead and discuss those matters in a debating fashion. Now that the subject of that debate has been discussed we can go on with another one, and I hope there will be no criticism about taking up time.
I am sorry the minister is not here today but I am sure that his parliamentary secretary, who is very faithful in his attendance and who is present, will take note of what is said and transmit it to the minister. The first thing I want to refer to is the general direction of the department. When the minister was first appointed there was a great surge of hope that perhaps he would initiate some new direction into the department, some new policies, particularly on immigration, which is a very difficult subject, and that a real effort would be made to start off in a postive direction on the question of immigration.
The minister has issued quite a number of very interesting press releases, including copies of speeches he has made; and since I have been charged with looking at these on behalf of the official opposition, I have read them. The releases and speeches are very nice and polite, but I have been unable to find any statement of policy, any indication of direction of policy, any statement as to what the minister or the government intends to do about immigration, citizenship or Indian affairs. The direction we are looking for has not been forthcoming, and we have been unable to decide in what direction the minister is going to move.
Therefore my first comment is that we are disappointed that we have nothing to criti-

Interim Supply
cize. It is the duty of the opposition to criticize the actions of the government if they are not what we think they should be, but when there is no policy, no direction, there is very little on which to comment. However, I think I can find a few things to say today about the department, perhaps more by way of criticism of lack of action than criticism of action. I feel that the minister either is saying nothing about his intentions or he has nothing to say. We hope that very shortly he will let us know what he intends to do with regard to his department.
I should like to turn first to what is probably the most critical and most difficult subject in the department, the question of Indian affairs. It is a subject which is not included in the title of the department, but I feel that at the moment it is the one which demands the most attention. In recent times we have seen a real stirring among the Indian people of Canada such as has never happened before. They want the opportunity to share in the development of Canada's future. It is very true that there is uncertainty as to the direction they are following. Many of the traditional chiefs fear that moves that may be made can only be in the wrong direction. This has resulted from the many years of paternalism on the part of the federal government and the Indian agencies. The chiefs in general are often afraid that a step taken will be in the wrong direction rather than forward.
We have heard quite recently of a number of things that have happened which indicate that the Indian people are finally going to make a move toward gaining their independence. There is one very significant factor at this time. I refer to the meeting of the chiefs at Garden River reserve in northern Ontario. There has been a good deal of quarrelling and bickering at this conference, and I suggest that if they quarrel and bicker enough they will qualify to join us here. More than that, Mr. Chairman, I feel that they should have the right to join us here. I suggest that seats should be found in this house for representatives of the Indian people of Canada.
A few years ago the former Conservative government gave the vote to the Indians of Canada. That was a move in the right direction. I think it was appreciated, and in my view the Indian people took advantage of it. However, this merely represents an ability to elect whoever runs within constituencies which already exist and have been established under redistribution. But I believe

for too long we have discussed the affairs of the Indian people in their absence, and I suggest that if they had a representative in the house it would be meaningful and we would be doing something to improve the situation of the Indian people.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Maybe it is a question I was about to answer, but go ahead.
