Is the hon. member aware of the fact that in the province of British Columbia a native Indian has been elected to the legislature in the same way as all the other members?

I am aware of that fact, and I think it is a good indication. I was about to say that an Indian had been elected as a member of a legislative assembly, but not as a representative of the Indian people. What I am suggesting is that the Indian themselves should elect one or more members from the Indian bands, and that those members should sit in the House of Commons as representatives of the Indian bands as a constituency of parliament. I was about to answer a question which might be raised. Why pick out the Indians from among the other racial groups in Canada to have their own representation, when there are so many racial groups in Canada? Any one of them might come along and say "We want to have our member of parliament".
The situation in connection with Indians is very different. In the first place, they are not subject to the same rules that apply to other people in Canada. Indians on reserves are confined to some extent in their activities, and are governed by the Indian Act and a number of other statutes. Their great effort is to be able to do what other ethnic groups in Canada can now do, become a part of the Canadian nation. But before they can do that there must be amendments to the Indian Act, or possibly repeal of the Indian Act.
The difficulty over the years has been that the Indians are in scattered groups. When the white man came to this country he scattered the Indians into small groups of people on small non-productive reserves where they became isolated from other people of their own race. It is only in recent times that conferences of the Indian chiefs have been convened, where they can come together and discuss their problems.
I think this is a tremendously good thing, and I was very pleased to see that the council of Indian chiefs was holding a meeting in

Ontario. My suggestion is that perhaps through this organization they should arrange for an Indian person to represent the Indian people in parliament so as to bring the voice of the Indian people before parliament with specific reference to their problems and the amendments to the act that are required. As I say, they have a different problem because they are governed and ringed about by special acts which apply to no other groups in Canada.
There is another encouraging sign which I am watching with interest, as are all other members. A young lady by the name of Kahn-Tineta Horn is raising her voice against what has been happening to the Indians of Canada over many years. Now, her voice is certainly not the unanimous voice of the Indian people as far as we can tell. Nevertheless I think the fact that she is speaking out and speaking loudly on behalf of the Indian people will serve as a catalyst to bring those people who support her views and those who oppose them to public attention. Perhaps the result will be to unite the Indian people so they can indicate to members of parliament what they really want in Canadian society. If these are the rules, so be it. I do not happen to agree with them but when a set of rules has been laid down I think they ought to be followed. We know for example that the Ralliement Creditistes do not

meet at least three of the conditions that have been laid down for the giving of political broadcasting time but, what is even worse, how did the corporation allocate the time? They have more members; they should have got more than 50 per cent.

I point out to you, Mr. Chairman, the provision under which the C.B.C. gives free political time to provincial political parties in a program which is called "Provincial affairs". In so far as the allocation of time for national affairs is concerned, this is the way it is divided: The chairman, that is Mr. Reeves Haggan, suggested that the C.B.C. formula would be as follows-this suggestion was made on November 14, 1963-Liberals, 7i periods; P.C.'s, 6J periods; N.D.P., 3; Social Credit, li and Ralliement Creditiste, 1J. These periods, as hon. members know, are 15 minutes each. Now, Mr. Chairman, if that kind of allocation is fair in terms of one elected body, surely it should apply to other places as well, inasmuch as we are dealing with a public corporation. One of the conditions, namely No. 4, is that a party must have a representative in the House of Commons to get any time at all.
Twelve members or more.

It does not say so; it says, "must have a representative." There was a case in which there were no representatives.
This points up something we in this party have believed for a long time. What has happened time and time again, and what has happened with regard to the way the

The fact is we do represent a portion of the Canadian people both in provincial and national affairs and this fact has to be respected.
Apparently, Mr. Chairman, this Reeves Haggan has a great deal to do with the allocation of time to political parties.

The minister says no. Well, the minister should familiarize himself with what is going on in that department.

Now, sir, this is the kind of attitude we cannot tolerate on the part of our public officials.
Ask for his resignation.

We can ask for his resignation and we can certainly insist that he be transferred so he will not have any responsibility for this matter. How can a man like this deal with political parties and the allocation of time if he displays such a bigotted attitude?
There is more to it than that. There has apparently been an order given somewhere in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to throw down a blanket of silence on the news broadcasts of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation respecting members of this party. I turn back only to last Tuesday night. There were two rather important matters that happened in this House of Commons. One of them had to do with the recognition of that great statesman of this century, Sir Winston Churchill. The other one had to do with a statement that was made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce respecting capital investment in Canada. I watched the C.B.C. television news very carefully that evening, and all the parties with the exception of the

Social Credit party were mentioned when they dealt with the matter of capital investment in Canada. As a matter of fact, the only member in addition to the Prime Minister who had anything at all to say about this parliament recognizing Sir Winston Churchill was the hon. member for Red Deer, and this fact was not mentioned at all.
These are examples of what we have seen for several months. I have listened to the news broadcasts over both radio and television and it is certainly obvious that someone in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has given a directive that there shall be a complete blackout of news respecting members of this party. It just so happens that we do represent constituencies and that the people in those constituencies pay just as much of the cost of operation of public corporations as the constituents of any other members in this house. The C.B.C. therefore has no right to discriminate in this manner against any of the parties.
It is true.

It certainly is true. We have noticed this time and again. I have in my file references to instances where there have been newsworthy stories filed by reporters for the C.B.C.-I do not blame them because they probably wrote the stories and somebody else partly cancelled them out-in which there have been no references to the members of this party. I am not trying to hold up the members of this party as being more newsworthy than anyone else. However, there have been times when a subject matter has been initiated by members of this party, and there has been no mention of them at all as participants in the story when the news has been broadcast.
We are seeking a committee, Mr. Chairman. We have had enough of it. We want to find out who gives these directives. In addition to that, we want the ministers to answer some of the questions that have been asked respecting the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. When it comes down to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's responsibility to parliament, I have talked to some of the officers of the corporation. I have tried to find out how members of parliament can communicate with the corporation, make their wishes known and give some direction to the corporation inasmuch as it is directly responsible to parliament. They say "It is very simple; if you do not like what we are doing, you can fire us."
I ask you, Mr. Chairman, is that a sensible, reasonable way to operate one of the largest

crown corporations in the country? You either turn over to them $75 million or $80 million and they spend it the way they like, without any direction from this parliament, or the only recourse we have is to fire them. No, that is not a satisfactory way of operating a corporation of this magnitude. There is another sound, sensible way. However, if that is the only recourse we have, Mr. Chairman, if that is the only recourse for members of parliament, then we had better start to do some firing because it is rather obvious from what is in the index pages of Hansard for this session and last that members of parliament are not happy with the way the C.B.C. is operating. If there is no other recourse, we had better start firing them; but there must be a better way than that of setting up rules and regulations.
I suggest, and in fact I demand on behalf of this party that we set up a committee on broadcasting composed of members of this House of Commons, notwithstanding the fact that there has been some kind of advisory committee on broadcasting set up. If I have time, I should like to refer to some of the terms of reference with respect to this committee, as follows:
To study, in the light of present and possible future conditions, the purposes and provisions of the Broadcasting Act and related statutes and to recommend what amendments, if any, should be made to the legislation-
Then it goes on:
-including an appraisal of the studies being made by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation of its structural organization; and including an inquiry into the financing of the C.B.C.-
And so on. If the C.B.C. is to be responsible to this parliament, surely the logical committee to hold an inquiry of this nature would be a committee of members of this house, and we demand that such a committee be established.
I see that the parliamentary secretary to the minister who answers for this corporation is here in the house. To get back to this Couchiching conference, we want to know how much the C.B.C. paid to the Canadian institute on public affairs. How much is given on a continuing basis; how much is given for the Couchiching conference and what does it cost the corporation to broadcast what is coming out of that conference? There was an hour of television last Saturday night, another hour on Sunday night and, in addition, an hour on the radio network of the corporation every night this week. How much are we paying for this kind of action? I may say I have listened carefully to some of the

reports and discussions which have come out of this conference and to date I have not heard one new idea as to what should be done to reform parliament. Not one suggestion has come out of there which the committee on procedure and organization is not fully aware of. I may say to these self appointed intellects that a full study has already been made of what ought to be done to improve parliamentary procedure. That is not the problem. The problem as I see it, and this has been very clear to members of the committee on procedure and organization, is to get parliamentarians to accept certain of these proposals. Whether or not recommendations are brought forward as a result of the profound and perceptive studies of these people will really make no great difference as far as practical improvements are concerned. It so happens that the members of this house are still in command, I hope, of the standing orders and whatever amendments to procedure may be made. I see my time is about up. There are one or two things I still want to say. There are many other facets of the C.B.C. that I wish to discuss when the time comes. But I wish to make it clear, now, that we are not satisfied with the way things are going. We believe there is rank discrimination shown by some of the officials of the corporation. We are not happy with the kind of culture they are trying to force down the throats of the Canadian people and we demand a committee of this house so that we can examine this question and set up a new kind of organizational structure to make sure that the C.B.C. will truly be responsible to the parliament of this country.

Does the hon. member belong to that school of Social Crediters who, in 1935, enacted legislation to control the press and radio, which legislation was later on declared ultra vires by the Supreme Court of Canada?

If I have any time left, I should like to say to the hon. member that I never did subscribe to that act, and of course the act was not as it is purported to have been by the hon. member. I am glad to have this opportunity to follow the discussion which was opened by my hon. friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka on some of the aspects coming under the purview of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, and to follow up some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Churchill concerning the Indian affairs branch. If such a discussion had not been initiated by them I would have been obliged to bring it up myself, because it is the subject of so many observations and comments which are made to me. In the region of Saskatchewan which I represent we are fortunate in having a resort area which is a great tourist attraction. Many of the comments made by those who visit this area concern the Indian population, and a good number of them reach my ears directly through private conversations. In particular, there is one resort project which has cost the public hundreds of thousands of dollars. It has wonderful lawns and trees and every facility for entertainment. A short distance away there is an Indian reserve. Many of the tourists use the road adjoining the reserve and they cannot help but notice the marked difference between the resort area and the reserve. Hundreds of thousands of dollars have been spent in one area, and obviously very little on an area the boundary of which is only a few yards away.
I am pleased, of course, to note that the department is taking action to correct some of the inequality which exists between the opportunities and standards of Indian citizens and those of citizens of other parts of Canada. The sum of $3J million has been referred to, this amount to be spent over three years. I would suggest it is going to take a lot more than $3J million to improve the conditions of Indians to any great extent. By the time this money has been dissipated all across Canada it will have very little effect.
Of course there are some parts of the country which are better prepared than

Interim, Supply
others to provide employment for Indians. In eastern Canada, where the economic situation is relatively stable and people are often able to work for 12 months of the year, the Indians no doubt avail themselves of the job opportunities open to them. But in Saskatchewan the situation is different. There is very little employment available to Indians during the winter, and this picture of part time employment is probably why the Indians in that province in many cases lead a hand to mouth existence. Any program to assist Indians should be discussed not only with the chiefs of the band councils but also with the welfare departments of the various provincial governments. These welfare departments are making a great contribution at the present time to improving the living standards of the Indians and it would certainly be to the advantage of federal officials to discuss with them the programs by means of which they hope to assist in further improving Indian living standards.
In past years in our province there have been meetings arranged by the Indians themselves. There is the Saskatchewan federation of Indians which meets annually. It is addressed by various prominent figures and dignitaries who always make a considerable contribution. Out of those conferences sometimes come some good ideas, and possibly it might be well to examine some of them with the idea of putting them into effect.
There was a brief presented some time ago which suggested that Indian chiefs be paid as overseers on the reserve, which would give them some insight as to what might take place at a future time and an insight into the role of municipal government. It does not matter how much money is spent on these reserves; it is hardly likely they will ever be in a position to support at any high standard of living the populations that live on them. The investment we make in the education of Indians will pay many more dividends than providing housing or other amenities.
In the past few years grants amounting to $350,000 a year have been paid by the federal government through the Indian affairs branch to improve housing on the reserves in my province. It has been suggested that it would take twice that amount, over several years, to bring the standard of living up to that which would be reasonably acceptable to anyone living in any other part of the country. Actually the unsuitable housing and accommodation provided has been an incentive to some Indians to leave the reserves. Some consideration should certainly be given to en-

deavouring to assist Indian families which have moved to urban areas and have found difficulty in meeting the high cost of rent, fuel, light, etc. out of the income they are able to secure.
The situation arises where the breadwinner of the Indian family is incapable of earning a sufficiently high income, due to inexperience and the standards required by employers. In many cases we find that the Indian's fear of losing his treaty rights has tended to influence his thinking, especially when he is giving consideration to returning to his home after a prolonged stay in an urban area. Many of us know of families which have returned to the reservation rather than face up to some of the financial difficulties they have found themselves in from time to time. It seems to me that the Indian affairs branch must take a good, hard look at their administrative policies and endeavour to come to grips with these alarming problems which the Indians face and which cause them to return to their reservations, where they find they are free of all financial worries, are maintained through no effort on their part, and are assured of all their rights provided by treaty, such as freedom from taxation, free medical care and clothing and all the other amenities which they enjoy. In other words, our reservation Indians find that living on the reserve rids them of all responsibility for their personal welfare, in comparison with having to work for these things while residing away from the reserve.
I suggest to the minister and his parliamentary secretary that the Indian affairs branch should endeavour to work out some solution of this problem by authorizing field officers to assume responsibility and assure the Indian family that they will be given every reasonable assistance to enable them to continue to reside on the reserve during the short periods each year when employment is not available or the income from employment will not permit them to meet reasonable costs of living. The agency superintendent should have full and proper authority to visit Indian families within his agency and assist them up to the amount the superintendent and the Indian affairs branch have arrived at, so that the family will have sufficient money to tide them over periods of unemployment or low income. We should take some responsibility to maintain the family in this way until such time as the breadwinner can either obtain better paying employment or find some other means of sustaining himself and his family. The cost

to the Indian affairs branch in providing such assistance would prove much less than the cost involved when the family returns bag and baggage to the reserve and again becomes totally dependant on the administration for their fuel, clothing and all the other needs.
Fortunately, as I have indicated, integration of the Indian has not been a problem, except in one instance. I refer to a specific local area in the town of Fort Qu'Appelle, where the department operates an Indian hospital. This is the only place in which we have segregation. It is odd that when we now have in Saskatchewan a provincial hospitalization plan and the provincial medical care plan, and the Indian is able to be received in the hospital of his choice, we bring patients from all over the province and treat them in the Indian hospital, especially those patients who have tuberculosis. I am glad to see the Minister of National Health and Welfare here, because she has received representations from this area on this particular topic. We are treating about 50 patients there at the present time, while three miles away there is a provincial sanitarium which is not being used to full capacity. It seems to me there is a duplication of service here, especially when there is a shortage of nurses, and that something more practical could be arranged in so far as these t.b. patients are concerned.
When we are dealing with the Indian problem we find that even among the Indians themselves there are sometimes second class citizens. I refer to those Indians of the Sioux tribe who came across the border many years ago looking for a place in which they could live in freedom and dignity after certain little indiscretions on their part at the time of the Custer massacre. They are here in Canada now, but they do not enjoy some of the privileges which are enjoyed by other Indians. They do not participate in the provisions of section 71 of the Indian Act. I doubt if they will ever receive any compensation from the Indian claims commission. They are settled on unproductive land and are not in the same position as Indians of some of the other tribes. It is in cases like this that I hope the money which is going to be used in the measure the minister calls the community development program will be applied. Surely, Mr. Chairman, an aroused public opinion will make it possible for us to erase some of these aspects of the question which I have mentioned, when we live in such an affluent society and spend so much money on entertainment, liquor, travel and tobacco. Surely 20220-396

Mr. Chairman, in taking part in this debate I hope I will be able to add some constructive ideas for the consideration of the department of immigration, with special reference to Indian affairs. I regret very much that the minister is not here this afternoon. However, I see that his parliamentary secretary is here and I hope that any suggestions I may offer which may be of some value will be conveyed to the necessary authority in the right way.
It is certainly not my intention to prolong the subject of immigration in the debate today, but I feel that this department should definitely make a more concerted effort to encourage immigration into this country, particularly from Great Britain, northern European countries and also from central Europe. I do not in any way suggest that I am opposed to immigration from other countries not included in that group, but I do feel that immigration from those countries should be maintained in its present form. However, I feel that the other group of northern European countries is not receiving active encouragement. I have this information from very reliable sources and I feel it is something which we should correct in the interests of our country. There are many people in those countries who could improve our trades, our industrial and our professional developments, and I know these people would be welcome.
When I compare the activities of this country to those of others to encourage these people to migrate, it seems to me we are very inactive or apathetic, and almost antagonistic. I have every reason to believe that in many cases people trying to enter our country are not encouraged to do so. In fact, the red tape they are faced with discourages them to such extent that the majority of this particular group go to Australia. I also have very definite information from certain of these east African countries, where a great number of the white settlers at the present time are leaving for other areas owing to the unstable political situation, that there is no effort whatever on the part of our government to see that these people come to Canada. In fact I understand that the television and radio advertising in these countries maintains a steady stream of encouragement to those people to emigrate to Australia. I cannot see why we in this country should not be doing more to encourage this type of

Interim Supply
citizen who would help develop our country, which is what we want at the present time.
It is obvious that these people have a great deal to offer our country, and with the proper qualifications would be able to improve our industry and many of our trades and occupations. They will help to create new industries and in that way improve our unemployment situation. I do not see how we can possibly associate our present unemployment situation with the fact that new immigrants will increase unemployment. This is not the case. The main burden of my remarks this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, is devoted to our native citizens, our Indian population, and some of the problems associated with them. I realize other speakers have mentioned several matters in this regard, but I feel there are some features which have not been brought out and which I should like to bring forward.
It has been my privilege over the years to watch the development of a great number of these Indian peoples, and I must say that the great change which has occurred among these people is not only encouraging but in some cases almost spectacular. In view of the fact that I have over 7,000 native citizens in the constituency of Kamloops I am naturally interested in their welfare.
There is no doubt, on looking back over history, that the grandparents and the great-grandparents of the present rising generation were looked on as second class citizens. A great deal of this has been the result entirely of a lack of education. Today I am pleased to say that this situation no longer exists and that some of our brightest citizens-and I mean that-are the well educated people of Indian ancestry. We must learn to recognize this great people. We must not continue to think that they are just wards of the government and second class citizens.
It has been my privilege over the years to have sat in conference with some of these people, some of whom have been university graduates, and I can tell you, Mr. Chairman, that their presentations and discussions have Deen equal to, and in many cases superior to, those of the non-Indian people. In the last few weeks in this House of Commons we had the privilege and honour of having in our presence the Canadian mother of the year, a lady from a reserve adjacent to my

own city of Kamloops. Anyone who has had the privilege of meeting this lady will recognize that her dignity, her poise and her high intelligence has created a most favourable impression. She is indicative of the possible development which is latent in these citizens, and it is this point in particular that I wish to emphasize.
Education is the answer to many of the problems facing the Indian people today. I am pleased to say that at the present time 90 per cent of the Indian children of school age in British Columbia are attending school. There are approximately 11,000 attending schools in British Columbia, 5,000 of whom are attending non-Indian schools. There are about 150 of our Indian citizens attending vocational schools, where they are learning carpentry, electrical engineering, mechanics, welding and other vocations of that type. About 12 are attending university at the present time, and many citizens of the Indian groups in British Columbia are taking advantage of the university extension courses lasting about a week in agriculture and in animal husbandry. So these educated people are definitely showing tremendous improvement.
We have adjacent to the city of Kamloops what we call an Indian residential school for general education purposes. It is an excellent school, and other talents besides general education are developed. At the present time this school has developed one of the most outstanding-and I emphasize the word "outstanding"-groups of dancers which we have anywhere in Canada. This group of fine young people are in such demand that at the present time they are on a tour of Mexico.
They have also been requested to do a European tour. They are native ambassadors of our country and I hope we might be able to arrange for them to perform at the world fair. I do not know of any organization which it would be more appropriate to have on the world fair program.
In view of their fine attainments, in view of their natural talents, their interesting personalities and the good will they create everywhere, I found it most disappointing that they were refused assistance for their passage to Mexico, both by the Canada Council and the department of Indian affairs. It would seem to me that money could be spent much better on projects of this nature than on many others which we witness almost daily around us. I believe the department should give consideration to providing financial assistance for such efforts.

The present effort is being financed by private subscriptions from people in the Kamloops area, and when the dancers got to Mexico the Mexican government undertook to pay all their expenses while they are there. It is not a very complimentary thing when we find the Mexican government prepared to pay the expenses of these people from Canada when, at the same time, the Canadian government refuses to assist them in their own country. Therefore I maintain that education is the answer to our Indian problems, as it is to many other problems.
We should develop more agricultural training centres. The present industrial school in Kamloops could enlarge its services to provide short courses in agriculture for adult Indian people, and the adjacent dominion range experimental station could assist with education on range development. I also believe an economic adviser could be added to the service to help make the reserves function in a more economic manner. They are not self supporting at present but they could be made so with very little trouble. I realize a good deal of this work is being done by the local Indian agents and their staffs, but they have sufficient problems to cope with, without getting into this field of economic advice on agricultural projects on the reserves.
Agricultural development could be encouraged by making larger individual holdings. In many cases family holdings have been broken up through the generations and are now so small that they are economically impossible to operate. It seems to me that the way to handle the situation would be to pay off some of the members of a family living on an uneconomic holding, and train them for other employment. Some of the band funds could be used for the purchase of more basic herd cattle or other animals that would help make the larger holdings productive. All these are problems that could be dealt with by an economic adviser.
One of the most unfortunate problems facing the Indian population today is the difficulty in obtaining proper employment, even after education and training. This is largely due to a long time prejudice, but I am happy to see that this prejudice is gradually being broken down.
It is with considerable gratification I have noted that in the past few years a new organization has developed in the interior of B.C., known as the brotherhood of North American Indians, with the special purpose of acting as a liaison between the Indian and the employer. They are being assisted by what is known as the "Mika Nika" club. I 20220-3961
Interim Supply
understand the meaning of these words to be "me and you". This organization is composed of Indian people and white people interested in the welfare of the Indian people, interested in trying to encourage them in their education and in trying to find suitable employment for them when they are educated and trained. They are trying to overcome that racial prejudice which has existed for generations in Canada, and they are meeting with a great deal of success.
I believe such organizations should receive special consideration from the dominion government. They are doing great work in improving the status of the Indian people, making them better citizens, making them more economically independent, and any assistance which the dominion government could give to them would be to the economic advantage of Canada as a whole. My own impression is that the Indian people, with proper education and encouragement, can prove their ability to accept responsibility, but it is the duty of the government to assist this development in every way.
During the term of office of the previous government great strides were made in the right direction. School attendance was encouraged. Scholarships were greatly increased with the aim of developing many natural aptitudes. Artists, craftsmen and musicians were encouraged. Indians were given the federal franchise. New roads were opened in reserves and new irrigation projects were developed. The present government must continue that wonderful work.
We have heard much about the establishment of an Indian claims commission. This was something which was promised during the last election. Last year a bill was introduced in parliament, Bill No. C-130, but received only first reading. There were many features in that bill which will require correction before it is acceptable to the Indian people. Its intent was probably quite correct but it contained many provisions that, if not amended, would only create more confusion.
Many things were contained in the bill but I do not intend to discuss all of them. However, I should like to draw attention to one or two points in the bill as it was presented last year in the hope that when it finally comes before us for debate these corrections will be made. In the first place, it is impossible to produce evidence in writing of certain claims which arose long ago before the Indians knew how to write. We know that most of these agreements were verbal and we must not consider that such claims have to be submitted in writing. Any requirement that

Interim Supply
they must be submitted in writing would simply mean that legitimate claims could be denied. Their land, fishing and hunting rights must be protected and evidence by affidavit as well as evidence in other forms should be accepted as sufficient to establish their rights.
Another point in this regard is that they only have two years to file a claim with the claims commission. I would say that five years at least should be the minimum that should be allowed for these people to do this. The proceedings of the claims commission should also be made public and should be recorded for future reference. Proper counsel should be provided. Certainly under the present bill these people are not provided with counsel. Band funds cannot be expected to provide the money because in many instances the costs would be prohibitive. There should be a right of appeal from decisions of the commission to provincial courts and even to the Supreme Court of Canada if this is necessary in extreme cases.
I could enlarge on the features of this bill at great length, but these are just some of the suggestions I wish to offer. Personally, and I know I am expressing the opinion of many people, I am optimistic about the future of the Indians. I feel that with proper encouragement and assistance a large majority of them will be capable of taking their rightful place in our economy and society. Therefore all I ask is that the government see to it that they receive all the encouragement and assistance they deserve.

I am surprised at the failure of certain members to take part in the debate on interim supply. On Monday not one member from any group other than Her Majesty's loyal opposition took part in the debate. On Tuesday the hon. member for Kootenay West rose in his place to ask that members of the staff be allowed to go home because

the weather was so hot. On Wednesday the hon. member for Kootenay West took part, as did the hon. member for Medicine Hat and the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac. On Thursday the hon. member for Villeneuve took part and today a few Liberal members have taken part in order to discuss the operation of taxis at Malton airport. No Liberals are taking part in the debate on interim supply. No ministers are here to answer questions or to rise in their places and take part in the debate. It reminds me of what the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said on April 1, 1964, as found on page 1642 of Hansard:
-I want to say to the government that I hope the impasse into which the House of Commons has manoeuvred itself will be a lesson to the government not to bring in supplementary estimates and interim supply almost at the deadline, when parliament either has to rush through them without proper consideration or has to sit beyond the time when we intended to adjourn.
He went on to say:
Members of the house have a right to expect from the government a very clear explanation why these additional sums are needed.
That is what he said on April 1, 1964. Has anybody in that group taken part in the debate on interim supply? Have members of the other parties taken part to any great extent?
Did the hon. member for Port Arthur not speak on Monday?

I doubt it but I stand to be corrected. If he did, I will give him full credit. This situation makes me think that some sort of arrangement or deal has been made. I do not think this is the way the government or parliament should operate.
With these introductory remarks I should like to proceed to a few matters concerning the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. The constituency I represent has a cross-section of new Canadians within its borders, people who have come to that riding because of the great attraction of employment in industries, on farms and as domestics. These people have fitted into the community well. They are a warmhearted group and I have the greatest admiration for them and their ability to integrate into the Canadian way of life. They have come here through the immigration department and they are excellent citizens and are very welcome.
They break down into all the various ethnic groups. Of course the largest group in my riding would be the descendants of those who come from the British isles. The next largest
Interim Supply
group is the group from Italy, some 4,200 people. This loyal group of people of Italian origin has been known to me for a long time. I have grown up with them. They were my friends long before I entered this House of Commons. I think back to their parents who came to our community to help develop it. Those were the days before we had steam shovels and mechanical devices for digging ditches to put in waterworks and sewers. These people came to my community to help instal these water and sewage systems. From that early race of pioneer people you will find descendants in every walk of life. We have them in the medical profession, dentistry, architecture, law as well as in the business world, contractors, and so on. I often wondered how we would have developed that community, let alone the many communities in Canada, if it had not been for all these people who came to Canada, particularly those of the Italian race.
I think of the building of that great subway in Toronto. How could this have been completed without the help of the many new Canadians who came to this country? I should like to refer the members of the committee to the amendments to the Immigration Act introduced in 1959 by the former minister, Mrs. Fairclough, under which people could come into Canada by virtue of their skills and not have to wait until they were sponsored. In this group we have had many people, such as carpenters, bricklayers, plasterers and others. These people have added so much to the development of our country, lhis department of immigration is a very important one.
I should like now to mention some of the things which disturb these people to a certain extent. They become frustrated when they have to wait so long to have the people they are sponsoring admitted to Canada. Then, sometimes they get letters saying these people do not qualify, do not meet all the requirements or some other such statement is made. They are at a loss to know just why these people are unable to come. I believe the minister might be moving in the right direction if he had his officials at the office in which these applications are made tell the applicants that there is no opportunity or no possibility of going to Canada. Then they would not be living in false hopes, as many of these sponsored people are now.
We are being asked to look into the spending of this department; that is what interim supply is. You are asking us to grant money to pay bills. The Minister of Citizenship and

Interim Supply
Immigration is asking the committee to pass estimates totalling $81,011,420, which represents an increase of 14 per cent over the last year. This includes the supplementary estimates. Have we not got the right, as the official opposition, to ask why there is this great increase of 14 per cent? What does the minister want this money for, and how is it to be spent? There are many interesting things that come to light when one goes through the department estimates. For example, for travel and removal expenses, the minister is asking us to approve a vote of $1,183,085. This is just for removal and travel for people within the department. Then, telephone and telegraph we find amounts to a little over a quarter of a million dollars. Have we not the right to ask why an amount such as this is needed by this department. I am convinced that this represents extravagance. I know it does. There is a staff of about 5,000 people. Should we not stop and look at this?
In studying the public accounts in the public accounts committee the other day, it was drawn to our attention by the Auditor General that this department has accounts receivable to the extent of $511,004 and of that amount $186,346 is listed as uncollectable. Why can this money not be collected? It is the taxpayers' money, your money and my money. After investigating the matter a little further, I found the list went back to the last world war, about 1939, and this made up the three main items. There are many small items, but it is made up chiefly of assistance payments to immigrants and salary overpayments. These items are the larger items making up these accounts receivable which are uncollectable. This is a matter, as I understand it, where the minister should make a submission for parliamentary approval to have these accounts written off, if there is no other way of collecting them. In view of the fact some of these accounts go back to 1939, I think it is time the bookkeeping was put in order.
There are many interesting things which come to light when you go over the estimates of this department. I believe there is a great amount of overlapping in this department. When an immigrant arrives in Canada, he is looking for employment. He wishes to be placed in a job. The immigration officer in the area is responsible for placing him in a job. The national employment service is engaged in the same activity under the Department of Labour. Here we have direct duplication, one becoming a competitor of the other. For example, if the national employment of-

fice has a machinist who is looking for a job they go to industry to see if they can find him a job. Perhaps the immigration officer has asked the same industry if they had a job for a machinist. There is therefore overlapping here. I suggest to the minister that the national employment service is recognized as the government agency responsible for finding employment for people. I believe it would be more economical, more efficient if this agency looked after the placement of newly arrived immigrants.
Then we have the recommendation of the Glassco commission to the effect that the Indian affairs department should be transferred to northern affairs or to the Department of National Health and Welfare. There has been much said here today about Indian affairs, and I do not wish to pursue the matter any further. The Department of Citizenship and Immigration should act as agent for the Department of External Affairs. It seems only natural that the issuance of passports would work more smoothly under the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
There is another matter which is, I think, of interest, and it concerns the proposed immigration to Canada of a large number of farmers of European descent who were formerly farming in Algeria. These former residents of north Africa, some 900 in number, are known as Black Feet. They lived in former French-administered territory, but after the independence of Algeria had been declared in 1962 they moved to France. In France they were unable to make a satisfactory living, or adapt themselves to conditions there. A shortage of land was another factor which made them consider migration, principally to Canada and, in particular, to the province of Quebec. I know there is no breakdown in the figures available to the department to show how many, if any, of these people come from Algeria, but while in Algeria these people had a reputation which was not of the best. With their background and their record I think it questionable whether they should be encouraged to settle here, and I am wondering how they came to Canada and by whose authority. What questions were asked of them before they were allowed to enter this country? We are advised according to the Toronto Star of July 30:
Immigration Minister Rene Tremblay yesterday announced that on July 22. Canada and France exchanged notes concerning the immigration to Canada of French repatriates.
The Canadian note sets forth the assistance available to French agriculturalists, repatriated to France from former French territories in north Africa.

It was expected that 30 or 40 families will be selected this year, Tremblay said.
In what special category have these people been placed? They are all farmers who have failed to adapt themselves or find land and make a living in France, and it is estimated that a thousand of these farming families are now looking for opportunities in Canada. Farming conditions in Quebec at the present time are certainly not good and I ask the minister to give serious consideration to the question whether or not these people should be allowed to immigrate here.
There is another matter which has been brought to my attention in my riding. It concerns the admission to Canada of prospective fiancees. As members know, under the present regulations fiancees are granted temporary entry to Canada for a period of 30 days, an extra two weeks being provided for the completing of the immigration formalities. The immigration regulations provide that a resident of Canada, if he falls within a certain class, may sponsor the admission of an intending wife or husband. When an application is made to this effect it is understood that the parties to the proposed marriage have been personally known to each other for a period of time and have also corresponded during their separation. Immigration officers, it is said, take great care in establishing that a previous and sincere relationship has existed between the two persons concerned and that they have an actual intention to marry. As evidence of this, the sponsor is asked to present letters, photographs and so on received from the fiancee, as well as a statement from a priest or minister that there are no impediments of objections to the marriage. In addition, there must be a statement from a notary public that there is a clear intention of marriage. Only when these conditions have been satisfied is the application approved. Applications from persons who know each other only from correspondence are not normally accepted.
These are the regulations. But in practice the system is not working out as well as it should. I realize there are people coming here with the intention to marry who find themselves in a strange land among strangers, speaking a language not known to them, and this creates unexpected difficulties. The Catholic women's league of Canada has brought this problem to my attention. They say, in a petition, that this time limit of one month or 45 days is altogether too short for prospective fiancees to become well acquainted before marriage, and that its imposition results in
Interim Supply
the marriage of many people who are incompatible, resulting in lifelong unhappiness. So I suggest to the minister that when the act is amended this time limit be extended to at least three months.
I turn now to a problem which exists in the restaurant trade in Canada. I do not suppose there is any industry which is more hard pressed for help than is the restaurant industry today. In other years we have had a goodly number of immigrants to Canada who have been able to fit in with this restaurant operation. If we in Canada are to provide good accommodation and good eating houses for the travelling public and for those Canadians who wish to patronize these places, the government should be going out of its way to see what can be done to bring in more people to take up this particular line of work.
I would say in conclusion what I said at the beginning of my remarks. I am amazed there are not more elected members on the other side of the house anxious to scrutinize one of the most important parts of the operation of government, that is, the spending of money. I hope we shall hear also from some of the ministers of the departments which have been mentioned.

May I ask the hon. member a question? In his opening remarks he made reference to an amendment to the immigration regulations in 1959 which changed "race or country of origin" to "educational skills". I know the hon. member has had a lot to do with immigration in the area from which he comes, and I ask him this: Does he not find that no improvement has really been brought about by this change? Is it not his experience that the amendment is still being interpreted in a discriminatory manner, as was the original regulation? I am sure the hon. member, who has had experience in these matters, would agree with me that there is still discrimination exercised by means of this particular amendment, just as there was formerly.

I thought the hon. member for Hamilton West was rising to make a speech. However, I would say I have not experienced any great discrimination in that regard as far as it affects the people of my own riding. I have found it has been possible to bring into my area people with skills that are badly needed-and into all Canada for that matter-where previously, whether skilled or not, they were not able to come. Now, if

Interim Supply
a man has a skill he is as welcome as the flowers in spring to come to Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want the hon. member to misinterpret my question. I am not opposed to the amendment and the subjects that are regulated. I have already spoken in the house on this matter. I am saying that the regulation is still being used as a smokescreen, in many ways, to keep out a number of people, in the same way that the original regulation in the act was used in connection with race or country of origin.
I would think this is a matter my hon. friend could take up with the minister and help him put the right interpretation on the amendment of the act.
Just give them a few lessons over there.

Mr. Chairman, I, too, welcome an opportunity to fulfil my responsibilities as a member of this house and take part in the debate on interim supply. For many weeks I have been sitting in this house waiting for an opportunity to bring to the fore some of the problems of my particular area; but since this government has been very tardy in bringing forth the estimates of the various department an opportunity has not been provided before now to bring these matters to the attention of parliament.
I was very interested in one particular aspect of the speech of the hon. member for Wellington South when he spoke of this new policy, apparently, on the part of the government and read from a newspaper article that I believe was entitled, "Path cleared for farmers to immigrate". As one who comes from an area where the farming is very intensive, and the tendency today is to have larger farms and smaller number of farmers engaged in this industry, naturally I am very interested in any change of policy in the matter of immigration. I wish to state at the outset that the remarks I propose to make should in no way be construed as a direct criticism of the people involved, their skill or their desirability as immigrants to this country; rather, I wish to speak on the principle involved in this question. It says in this article:
Canada and France have reached agreement on the conditions under which French farmers repatriated to France from former French territories in north Africa may enter Canada as immigrants.
I am indeed sorry that the minister is not in his seat today, because this poses a very, very serious question in my mind. I want to

know, what are these conditions, because later on in the article it says:
The department said no arrangements have been made as yet for initial arrivals-
All of the repatriates must comply with the provisions of the Immigration Act.
If this is the case, why was it necessary for Canada and France to reach agreement on the conditions? It is my understanding that it was very difficult for anyone to immigrate to this country from France, because of special conditions set up by the French government which prevented citizens leaving France and going to any other country. If this is the case, I would like to know why the government of France is ready to make an agreement with the government of Canada to allow these repatriates to enter this country. I wish to know, does this new agreement make it possible for any farmer in France, whether he be a repatriate or a native of that country, to immigrate to Canada?
Then, too, I am very interested in this article when it states that all these special services will be placed at the disposal of these immigrants to our country. I would like to ask the minister, what does this mean? Does it mean that these services are not at the disposal of all immigrants to this country and that these are special provisions made for these particular immigrants? What is the change of policy in this respect?
There is another matter I should like to inquire into. This article states:
Officials said that repatriates seeking admission to Canada as immigrants will receive suggestions on possible locations from French officials who toured Canada earlier this year.
I want to know about this. Were these French officials in Canada at the invitation of the Canadian government? Was special provision made to invite them to come to this country? Did they tour this country from coast to coast at the invitation of the Canadian government to see where these people might be repatriated in Canada; or is this a courtesy that is accorded to all nations, namely to send delegations to this country and tour it from coast to coast to see where immigrants might best be settled? These are some of the questions that are of particular interest to farmers across this country, who under the present administration are finding it very difficult to make a living because of the conditions under which they are forced to operate. How many of these people are supposed to enter this country? The article states that "30 or 40 families will be selected this year". It is the word "selected" that bothers me. Is there a special committee set up to

screen the abilities of these immigrants? How are they to be selected? What are the conditions they must meet before they can enter this country. Are they going to be treated differently from any other immigrants? Are their conditions of entry into this country any different?
These are questions to which we have a right to answers, having read this article headed, "Path cleared for farmers to immigrate". We want to know, is it cleared for farmers of all foreign countries to enter this country, or are these conditions set up for farmers of one particular country? I think we are entitled to have answers to these questions. Since we have not had an opportunity to raise these questions, I am sorry the minister is not in the chamber to deal with these serious doubts that arise in our minds.
These matters are brought to the fore in my mind because of the fact that we, as members of parliament, have serious problems in obtaining entry into this country of people who apply to us directly. There are conditions-and naturally there must be conditions-under which immigrants enter Canada; and these conditions must be met. But it seems unjust when people who have been admitted to this country and have lived here in a law abiding manner are turned down when they apply for citizenship. I know of one case where the person applied perhaps four or five times for citizenship. It is not easy, when you are in an adopted country, to go before a court and be refused citizenship. This is a matter of shame as far as some citizens are concerned. Law abiding people who try to obtain Canadian citizenship and are refused often find their neighbours and friends of their basic origin tend to look down on them as being undesirable. Surely they should be told something else, when their application for citizenship is turned down, other than the terse statement that they fail at this time to meet the requirements. This has happened time and time again in the area that I represent, and these people find it very difficult indeed, because of the shame they feel or the way in which they are treated by their friends.
Another question in this respect involves principle. I refer to a young lady who wished to come into this country as a domestic. It is true that she is coloured, but that had no bearing on her immigration to this country.
In this case I speak of a doctor who had gone to a foreign country and this young lady, a well educated young lady, worked for him and his wife while he was there. She did so
Interim Supply
in such manner that they became enamoured not only of her personality but of her devotion to duty and wished to bring her to this country. They went to the local office, and they were assured that all the conditions had been fulfilled; but when they came to this country they found the conditions were far from fulfilled. After waiting many months they were told this lady could not enter the country. They made representations to me and I, of course, brought the matter to the attention of the minister-and I must thank the minister for his courtesy in this respect. I have since received a letter to the effect that this domestic did not meet the requirements of the immigration department because of the fact that she was uneducated.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I can understand that this is a necessary requirement, but when I looked further into the matter I found that this lady was not only educated but that she had attended the church school in her own particular area and was something of a scholar. One application after another has been made but in each case a different reason advanced as to why she could not enter the country; and after many months I might point out that she has still not been allowed to enter the country.
I should like to bring to the attention of the committee that last week end I was privileged to have the opportunity to attend a Slovac picnic of an international nature held in my riding, and it was inspiring indeed to hear the many learned speakers who took part on the program. It was very inspiring indeed to spend the afternoon watching the young folk with their native dances and in their native costumes. I am sure that every member of this committee would have been proud to listen to the tenor of the speeches made at that picnic. These people were grateful to be citizens of Canada. They were grateful to have had the opportunity to come to this country and to live and work in this country. One thing which made an impression on me was that they were instilling in their young people not only a love for this country but a respect for this country. They were trying to instil into their young people the good traits and qualities and the high principles of their native land, so that they could make a contribution of a greater nature as citizens of Canada in a new country. This is a fact to be commended and we need have no doubt for the futures of the children of these people.
Another matter I should like to deal with has to do with Indian affairs. I have not had the opportunity before now to pay tribute to a

Interim Supply
particular gentleman. I must assure the committee that I have no idea where he is today. I have no idea what he is doing. But I am sure that no matter where this man is or what he is doing he is contributing as an Indian to the welfare of the Indian nation and to the welfare of this country as a whole. This is the nature of the man. I had the opportunity of meeting this man when he was an Indian agent on the Indian reservation in my riding of Kent, Ontario. It was inspiring indeed to see the manner in which this man approached the very basic problems of the Indian nation and tried by all manner of approach to do something about them. This man had the welfare of his nation at heart and did much to raise their lot while he was there as an Indian agent. This particular reservation is one of the first to be granted control of its own affairs. It was one of the first to form a band council to elect its own officers. It was one of the first reservations which did without an Indian agent, and there is no Indian agent at the present time on this particular reservation. Because of the training of these men and the competence of the Indian affairs branch in their welfare, they manage their own affairs in a very commendable way. Much of the credit must go to this man, Mr. Powless, for whom I have the greatest admiration and respect, for the principles he instilled in his people.
As far as Indian reservations are concerned, I can only speak with regard to the one in my constituency. I speak now as one who has farmed. On this particular reservation there is some of the finest land. Mr. Powless and his administration have brought this matter to the attention of the band. But like all good land in this country, if it is not drained and cultivated with the proper machinery it cannot bring forth the best possible amount of produce and be economical to farm. If it were possible to carry out on this reservation the programs laid down by this same Mr. Powless, the progressive dreams which he started to carry out under the winter works program of the former government, such as cutting down trees, digging ditches and making roads, the whole community would benefit. This program was bringing this reservation out of the wilderness and making the people feel self sufficient. If this policy could be carried on the young men on this reservation would not be so anxious to go to neighbouring cities and towns to obtain employment. They would have the opportunity to farm this land as the farms around them
[Mr. Danforth.l
are farmed. All they need is machinery and capital. They need someone who will show them what could be done and how to do it. That is where they miss this wonderful Indian agent, because he had the vision. He could see that the people could obtain their independence. They are not people of charity, they are people of courage, and if they have the tools to work with they can do the job. They are people who, when given the opportunity, will make the finest of Canadian citizens.
One thing I am very glad to see is that the Indian children on that reservation do not go to their own local school but instead are taken by bus to the community school. They are mixing with other young children in the district and becoming friends and neighbours, and a greater feeling of good will is developing between the two groups than before. That is a fine thing and I should like to see this work continued in this particular area. Surely to goodness if these people want to work-and all they need are the tools-this is one action we can take to help them make the living they deserve.
In dealing with these particular programs I feel that the people in Kent county, who are of various nationalities, show to the country as a whole and to the world what can be done by people of all nationalities working together. We in Kent county have immigrants from practically every nation in the world, all of them working together in harmony. I am very proud to say that in Kent county we have a situation which is an example to the Dominion of Canada today, because we have 11,000 French of whom we are most proud working with Anglo-Saxons, Italians, Germans, Dutch, Slovacs, Czechs, and Hungarians in absolute harmony. In Kent county, sir, there is no such thing as a second class Canadian or a hyphenated Canadian, and when Canada as a whole is like that this will be a Canada of which we can be really proud.

Mr. Chairman, before I begin the few remarks I wish to make, I should like first to bring to the attention of the house a correction I want to make in Hansard in order to put the record straight.
Yesterday, in his remarks, the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Moreau) said, according to page 6206 of Hansard'.
I would like to point out that the hon. member was not present when the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources were being discussed last Friday.

Now, Mr. Chairman, if you refer to page 5938, you will see that my name is on the list of those who voted and that, a few minutes later, when the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources were called, I also was in the house.
I would, therefore, ask the hon. member for York-Scarborough to check the facts before making statements.
I must repeat that we are now considering estimates totalling $700 million, that is, almost three quarters of a billion dollars, that the government is asking us to pass. If we were to listen to the hon. members opposite, we would comply with such a request without taking the trouble to study it.
Since the beginning of this debate four days ago, we tried to obtain information from four different ministers. First of all, we were unable to get any information at all from the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen).
Realizing our inability to break the silence of the Minister of Labour, we turned to the Department of National Health and Welfare, but the same thing happened. We then turned to the Department of Forestry but, to make sure that he would not have to give any information the minister left for Europe on a holiday. Today we are studying the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration; once again the minister is away. Has he gone on a holiday too? That is possible.
Not at all.

In any case, we will keep on going; even if he is not on holiday, he is not in his seat where he should be to fulfil his responsibilities.
Mr. Chairman, I ask our hon. friends
opposite to shake, once and for all, that carelessness which befell them and to realize finally that it is their duty to take part in this debate. Let the ministers show a little less complacency and let them stop considering with unequalled jauntiness and impatience the questions directed to them. It is their responsibility to give here the information requested from them.
If I rise again today it is in an attempt to get other information with regard, in particular, to the farm people in my riding and in eastern Canada-
Read the copy of the Globe and Mail I am sending you.

Mr. Chairman, if I thought you could have the least bit of influence on the most delinquent member of the house, I would ask you to call to order the hon.
Interim Supply
member for Lotbiniere who is here today. This is one of the rare occasions when he shows himself in the house but since we want to maintain some sense of propriety we will put up with his insubordination.
No, no.
However, Mr. Chairman, following-

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege merely to say that I appreciate the hon. member's humour because I am a man who likes humour. Besides, he is the exact opposite of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), who is always raging. I hold in esteem the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard), who is realistic enough and consistent in his statements. I nevertheless wish to tell him that I am an assiduous member of this house, despite the fact that he is hinting that I am always absent, whereas the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) himself, is never here. The statement made by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot is unfair.

Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that the hon. member cannot stand up for himself. He has to rely on others to justify his behaviour. Obviously, what he is saying will be printed in the record. But we realize that physically he is not here often and, as I said we very seldom see him in the house, today being a rare exception.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot is repeating the same insinuation. He is making the same statement which is contrary to the facts. I am in regular attendance at the sittings of the house and it is unfair for the hon. member to say that I am often absent from the house when I am one of those who attend the sittings most regularly. At the moment the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams), and the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) are all away on holidays. The hon. member is insinuating that I am the one who is absent when I am here and they are away.
That is not true, you are always absent.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I think the committee is getting into an argument that has

Interim Supply
nothing to do with the resolution before it. Hon. members' comments should be more in relation to the subject matter before us.
Mr. Chairman, I was interrupted by the hon. member for Lotbiniere for having spoken the truth.
No, no.
I see that the hon. member does not like the truth to be known. In that case I cannot but override his objection, and if I have hurt the hon. member by speaking the truth I have no apologies to make-
No, you are not telling the truth.
-as the truth must be told in any event but I shall not insist-
You are not telling the truth; I want my words to be printed in Hansard, because this is a false statement.

Mr. Chairman, I mainly rose this afternoon following an item published in Le Devoir of July 29 last, with regard to an agreement, and I quote:
Franco-Canadian agreement on the settlement in Canada of French farmers from Algeria.
And, before the hon. member for Lotbiniere interrupts me to say-in order to have it printed in Hansard-that I am against French immigration, I immediately state that I favour French immigration, but that I find the immigration of farmers to be established in eastern Canada not only upsetting, but inappropriate.
If you refer to the recently published Men-zies report, you will find that farming in eastern Canada is in a precarious, deplorable state-
"Depressed" is the word to use.

-in a depressed state. I know that my friends opposite deplore the fact that eastern farmers in Canada do not have adequate income to meet their obligations. Now, at the same time, the government that is presiding over the fortunes of the nation thinks it has found an adequate remedy to that poor situation by inviting farmers from abroad to come to this country in order to place them in the same position as those who are complaining that their income is inadequate.
According to the press release published in Le Devoir, which, I suppose, comes from [The Deputy Chairman.]
the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, that department has put at the disposal of the newcomers in Canada all the facilities of the department in order to help them to get integrated and to meet their obligations.
Now, if this government has money to settle foreigners in Canada, I submit it is our responsibility, we who are sitting here, and especially members from the province of Quebec, to see to it that those amounts be spent in the interests of our compatriots who are already settled on farms and who are facing numerous difficulties. We must discharge our obligations to those persons first. I know a great many young people who could not afford to settle on farms, and before going over to get Frenchmen, Englishmen and Dutchmen, or people of any other nationality, I say that the government should see to it that taxation money goes to our people first.
We have some responsibility toward our people. We should first of all discharge this responsibility, and our friends opposite, instead of pointing their fingers-
Hear, hear.

I see the hon. member for
Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Pepin) seated in his place, and I remember he had not the courage, last week, to come and vote in the way he had indicated he would. Outside the house he made, in blazing terms, speeches to the effect he would object to the government policy, and today as a prospective minister-

speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member is now commenting about a proceeding of this house that has already been concluded.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. In sound constitutional theory the parliamentary secretary has to be

jointly responsible with his minister in matters concerning the department, but he is free, as any other backbencher, in other matters.

Mr. Chairman, may I put another question to the hon. member? Did he express the opinion of his minister when on May 20 last, he said, in Drummondville, that we are experiencing the fall of the central government? If you refer to the newspapers you will see that what I am reporting is strictly correct.

So I ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Tremblay) who is absent- he is probably on vacation-to make sure that, first of all, we meet our obligations to our constituents, our fellow countrymen; then and only then let us continue to give away our surpluses and do our share in order to help the people of other countries. Would the hon. member allow me a question? Am I justified in concluding from his remarks that he stands against immigration of French as well as people of other nationalities?

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot spoke about my I.Q. I shall ask him to read his speech carefully on Monday. He might be disappointed. One must always think well before speaking.
