speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Fort William has the floor.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened to the debate on the Department of Citizenship and Immigration with a great deal of
Interim, Supply
interest. I was rather surprised, however, to hear the hon. member for Wellington South and the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) expressing grave doubts about the decision of the government to admit to Canada a number of French farmers, formerly residents of north Africa. It is quite evident that the minister's announcement of a few days ago has been misunderstood by the members opposite. I will therefore try to clarify the situation very briefly. I do not intend to make a speech but I believe this occasion should not be let go by without an explanation so that everyone will understand what the government is trying to do in this regard.
A few days ago the minister made an announcement regarding an exchange of notes which had taken place between the Canadian and French governments respecting the migration to Canada of French agriculturists who have been repatriated to France from former French territories in French Africa. As the minister mentioned in the announcement, it is expected that 30 or 40 families will be selected this year, with future movements being dependant upon the successful establishment of these first families, and individual decisions to be made in the future by others.
The exchange of notes set out the various forms of assistance which will be available to these agriculturists from both the French and Canadian governments. In essence the two governments will co-operate in the establishment of an information program designed to acquaint prospective settlers with conditions of life and opportunities for settlement on Canadian farms. The French government will assist in presenting suitable interested applicants at the Canadian immigration office in Paris, France, where they will be examined in accordance with established immigration criteria for the selection of agriculturists generally.
This means that all prospective settlers will have to comply with the normal immigration requirements including health, character, passports, etc., as well as being able to demonstrate by previous agricultural experience, adaptability and availability of capital that they will be able to operate an efficient farming enterprise by Canadian standards.
The Canadian government is not participating in or contributing to the financial arrangements respecting transportation and settlement in Canada apart from acquainting the settlers with the facilities available to all Canadian residents through the Farm Credit Corporation.

Interim Supply
Those settlers who are able to qualify under the immigration criteria set out above will have placed at their disposal the full range of services offered by the immigration branch to all newcomers to Canada. This includes reception on arrival and the extension of assistance in locating suitable areas of final settlement, as well as assistance in obtaining temporary accommodation and employment where required. In advance of any settlers coming forward, the Canadian government will make available full details of typical farm properties for sale in various regions of Canada which present conditions favourable to establishment. Experienced immigration settlement officers will also be available at all times to assist these agriculturists in the assessment and other aspects involved in the purchase of Canadian farms.
I am confident that all hon. members and Canadians generally will join with the Canadian and French government in wishing this venture every success.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Yes.

A while ago the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot said the minister was on a holiday, perhaps like the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and the hon. member for Bow River. Is the parliamentary secretary able to say where the minister is?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: The minister has gone on a very important mission, which is government work. He has taken on the responsibility of several engagements over the week end. I might say, for the benefit of the member, it is not a question of enjoyment of a holiday; it is a question of work.

I reluctantly enter this debate because of some remarks that have been made. First of all, I should like to offer a suggestion to which I feel the house should give some consideration and which I think merits the support of all hon. members. Here we are at the end of July faced with the estimates of a department, following the budget and the financial accounting by the government. However, at this time we have only passed the estimates of one department and this gives some credence to the fact that the departments that have not been brought before the committee bear some scrutiny. Six months is ample time for the government to do this. This situation raises a number of problems.

One of these problems has been solved in Great Britain by limiting one section of the parliamentary year to a consideration of financial business. When that is concluded, parliament goes on to the consideration of other matters. The operation of parliament here, of course, is very ragged. We have estimates, interim supply, supplementary estimates and the budget debate interspersed with legislative matters. I feel the time has arrived when we should set up a standing committee on estimates and refer each of the departments to that committee. This, of course, would allow members the free use of the parliamentary committee system. It would allow members to discuss individual problems they have which do not necessarily need governmental intervention, or are of a local or personal nature affecting the welfare of their constituents. It would allow also the opportunity to present a report which could contain certain recommendations to which the government would be obliged to give some consideration.
This procedure might also carry an obligation that members of parliament would not repeat in the house the problems of a local nature that they raised in the committee. I think it is time that parliament, and particularly the government, gave some consideration to adopting this procedure.
I am aware also that unless our parliamentary committees system changed, this would mean we would be running six or seven months on the estimates of the various departments. It might be necessary for members of the steering committee to give consideration to priorities for various departments. If they gave priorities, obviously this department would get top priority. Since I have been here, Mr. Chairman, I have been shocked at the things that go on under the table in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. I have always felt that one of the weaknesses was the minister. Certainly, the weakness has been repeated and magnified in the appointment of the present minister who made a statement not long ago that got me into a good deal of trouble. He told the house he had complete confidence in his officials. At the time I said he was the only one in the house who did have complete confidence in them. I think that was true. The next day I received a telephone call from the deputy minister of citizenship and immigration who told me, "You had a problem and you asked me to do something about it; you can forget about it now because I have no intention of answering your requests in the future."

If this had not been a telephone call that man would have been before the bar of this house because it certainly is a breach of his rights and privileges and a breach of my rights as a member of parliament.
In view of what the minister said, I should like to point out who this little god almighty is who sits in the seat of a senior civil servant in this department. He is a man by the name of Isbister. Isbister, according to Canadian Who's Who, is a B.A., Ph.D.; Canadian public service; economist and was born at Winnipeg, Manitoba in 1914. It goes on to say various things about him. He was a teacher of mathematics at the University of Manitoba,
1934-	35; did actuarial work for the Sun Life Insurance Company of Canada, Montreal,
1935-	39; instructor of economics, Harvard, 1942-45; assistant dominion statistician, bureau of statistics, 1945-47; assistant director, economics branch, department of reconstruction and supply, 1947-49; director, international trade relations branch, Department of Trade and Commerce, 1949-57; promoted to assistant deputy minister there, 1957-58. Then it goes on to mention Zea Psi -I suppose that is a club; Unitarian, his religion, and his club, Cercle Universitaire; home, 19 Madawaska drive, Ottawa.
You know, Mr. Chairman, there is absolutely nothing in there to warrant his being appointed deputy minister of citizenship and immigration. Then I should like to quote from an article in the Ottawa Journal, January 25, 1963 which says:
A former assistant deputy minister in the finance department recently suggested that out of clear compassion tenure of such office should be limited to three year periods.
Then there should be a measure of going out to graze, in some field of government where constant pressures are less.
This may be his interpretation of being a deputy minister in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, and I think it has been the opinion of several of his predecessors, but we are going to have a rotten mess in that department until we finally get somebody as deputy minister who will give some leadership and create for the department the respect which we have for every other department and its senior officials. I think he is in a class much below the average class of junior civil servants and that he has no right whatever to hold the office of deputy minister in that department.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
On a point of order, I think the hon. member is going beyond the point of good taste when he indulges in such a vicious attack on one of our senior civil
Interim Supply
servants. Whatever this gentleman's shortcomings may be, if there are any, the use of this type of language against one of our senior civil servants is not called for. I regret it very much and I would ask the hon. member in all sincerity to withdraw the remarks he has made about the deputy minister of citizenship and immigration.

I have no intention of withdrawing them and, what is more, the next time the estimates of this department come before us I will have his complete history and do the job which should be done with this type of civil servant. Let me tell you what the case was, Mr. Chairman. This was the case he told me he was not going to have anything more to do with. It concerned one of my constituents, a woman who has been living in this country for some 60 years and who has raised a family in my part of the country. Over a number of years she has been applying for citizenship, without success, probably-this is not within my own knowledge-because she had some connection with an organization which was not felt to be in her own interest or in the interest of the country. This happened, I understand, many years ago. I suggested that if this woman kept applying for citizenship, and if her applications were accepted by the local court, but rejected later by the department, why should the department not advise her that there was no point in her going through this process year after year, only to be turned down by the department. I suggested that if there was no intention of allowing her to become a citizen, then at least the department should have the courtesy to say she did not appear to meet the requirements and there was no point in continuing her applications. This was a simple case which arose in my own constituency. I believe this senior civil servant far overstepped the bounds within which he had responsibility in the remarks he made, and I believe there should be no discrimination against me, in respect to the normal relations I have with the department, on account of the observations I am making this afternoon on the floor of the house.
If this is the kind of civil servant we have in the department, I do not want this kind of civil servant, and I think every member of the house will resent the fact that such a statement has been made by him. I think it is wise to question whether this man is qualified or capable of holding his present position and I would like the parliamentary secretary to rise and tell us one good qualification

Interim Supply
In my opinion this will also involve the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, because I believe they play a large role in this matter. If the minister gives consideration to this request at all, I would like him to arrange for light to be shed on some of the operations of the department in this connection, because obviously the R.C.M.P., through their security and intelligence branch, must share some of the responsibility with the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. I have found that the problems I have come across with regard to citizenship have in many instances flowed from the reports made by the R.C.M.P. security and intelligence branch, many of them being years and years old.
I make these two requests, Mr. Chairman, and if this government does not want to get into trouble, I think they will give consideration to them. I honestly see the Department of Citizenship and Immigration as the weakest in our departmental system, the weakest department in the government today and the one that poses the greatest danger to the government if it does not face up to its responsibilities and do something to correct some of the ills of that department.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Brandon-Souris.
Carried.
Mr. Chairman, my first words must be of a complimentary nature to the hon. member for Port Arthur who has been following the course of this discussion with considerable interest.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Fort William.

Yes, the hon. member for Fort William, who has been following the course of this discussion carefully and has been sufficiently interested in this important debate to make an intervention. I know that the hon. member for Fort William is vitally interested in the subject of citizenship and immigration from a personal standpoint as well as from the standpoint of his responsibilities as parliamentary secretary to the minister. I am glad that at least one member of the government, one member of the Liberal party, is following the important discussion that is taking place. As I rose to speak, Mr. Chairman, I heard many voices from the other side saying "Carried".

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Hope springs eternal.

Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, I think this is just about the depth of the interest of the great majority of the

government supporters in this important subject. I am particularly amazed that these voices should be heard following the criticisms and accusations that were presented to this committee by the previous speaker, the hon. member for Timmins. He has made some serious charges.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Timiskaming.

The hon. member for Timiskaming, yes. He has made some serious charges and has put forward some helpful suggestions. He has made one helpful suggestion in particular with regard to a department of this importance. It is particularly important because it involves the basic rights of Canadians and fellow humans. He has suggested that this department be referred to a special committee on estimates so that it might be considered in depth. I hope, in view of the criticisms which have been made, that this recommendation will be put before the government and accepted.
I think it is a revealing commentary that this committee of the House of Commons should be considering interim supply on this last day of July, July 31. There was a time in the parliamentary process when estimates were given priority treatment, it being recognized that a careful scrutiny of the expenditures of government departments was one of the basic functions of the annual parliamentary session. This business of providing supply for Her Majesty based on the age old cry of freedom-no taxation without representation-has been ignored by the present government, as testified to by the fact that at this late date in the parliamentary year we have to resort to the procedure of discussing in depth the various departments on the government's motion for interim supply, which will enable the government to finance its operations on an emergency basis until such time as it can get approval of its main estimates.
I can remember the days in this house when the Liberals were in power almost in perpetuity and used to resort to the device of leaving estimates till the end of the parliamentary year.
That is better than not presenting any at all, as you did.

This was the procedure of the former Liberal government, based on the premise that the July heat would create a sense of urgency for the adjournment of parliament on the part of both opposition and government, with the result that the estimates

would be given the minimum of examination. And the government proceeded on that basis.
You did not present any for two years.

I shall deal with these interjections in a moment. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the new Liberal government, which my hon. friend from Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm refers to as the "same old bunch", is still in fact the same old bunch and has resorted to this threadworn method of leaving the estimates to the July heat in the hope that the opposition will fold their tents and quietly steal away, and will not cause too much concern to the government.
Is that why you did not present any?

However, I would remind hon. members opposite that they are not faced with a docile opposition. They are faced with a responsible opposition which recognizes as its chief responsibility the importance of scrutinizing estimates department by department.
I am equally amazed, Mr. Chairman, by the reaction of our good friends in the press gallery. I can remember 10 years ago, when we used to rush through estimates, the headlines were something to this effect: "Opposition neglects its responsibilities and fails to give proper attention to the careful examination of the estimates".
We are not on estimates.

My hon. friend, who has only been in the house two years, does not yet realize where he is. He says we are not on estimates. The other term for estimates is supply, in case he is not aware of it, and I think we are on interim supply at the moment.
The cry today is that examination of the estimates is obstruction-

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Boredom.

-and that is the sentiment which has been expressed by various public media across the country. The Minister of National Health and Welfare says it is boredom. If she can call the charge made by the hon. member for Timiskaming boredom, she is very derelict in her ministerial responsibility, particularly her responsibility for such a vital department as health and welfare, which overlaps citizenship and immigration in its concern for human welfare.
Interim Supply
There were one or two observations made from across the floor as I commenced my observations to the effect that it is better to present estimates late than not present them at all. I would remind hon. members opposite that that situation occurred during a period when the Conservative party was leading this house as a minority government and the avowed intention as expressed by the then leader of the opposition, now the Prime Minister, was to defeat the government by using every obstruction tactic available. That is on the record of Hansard and is indicative of the sort of irresponsible role which the opposition of that day performed.
We did that because you were not competent.
My hon. friends also intimate that they were protesting against an incompetent government of that day. My hon. friend in the back row-
Hamilton West.
My hon. friend from Hamilton West suggests that they were protesting the inadequacies of the government.
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I did not say that. They are the hon. member's words.

The protest at that time, Mr. Chairman, was to the effect that the Conservative party as a government was fiscally irresponsible and economically incompetent. We now know that as a result of the economic and fiscal policies of the former Conservative government Canada moved into an era of economic expansion which is unprecedented, and I am not just drawing that statement out of the air. If my hon. friend from Hamilton West will read the reports of the various banks, the economic analyses which come across his desk and will look at the statistical charts, he will find that they all concur with that viewpoint. As a matter of fact, just this morning while listening to the C.B.C. news report there was a statement to the effect that last year Canada enjoyed the largest increase in commodity exports in its history; I think the figure was 49 per cent. This was due to devaluation of the dollar, a step which was irresponsibly criticized by the irresponsible opposition of those days; when the gimmick of criticizing the so-called "Diefenbuck" became one of the chief propaganda tactics of that irresponsible opposition.
Having indulged in those preliminary remarks I return to the point I was making.

Interim Supply
that it is a revealing commentary that we have to resort to this method to carry out one of the most important functions of the parliamentary process. I trust that our friends who communicate what goes on in parliament to the public at large will stress the point, as they used to stress the point ten years ago when the opposition failed to deal adequately with estimates, that we are only discharging our responsibility in the best way we know how under the circumstances.
Again I would support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Timiskaming that a department as important as the Department of Citizenship and Immigration should come under careful examination in a committee on estimates, so that some of the criticisms levelled at the department could be dealt with fully. It certainly seems apparent we are not going to get any reply in committee of the whole, so the government should take it upon itself to be sufficiently responsible to provide some parliamentary medium through which replies and satisfactory explanations can be made to these observations.
I have long been interested in the work of the department. Up until quite recent times, there was no doubt about it that there was a discriminatory bias operating in the functions of the department. In the immediate post-war period, when there was a surge of humani-tarianism in reaction to the barbarism of world war II, the position of the department in respect to its processing of intending immigrants became increasingly inconsistent. It was becoming increasingly difficult to keep up the camouflage that no discrimination existed in the department.
Why do I say there was discrimination? Well, I refer to the immigration policy that was laid down by a former prime minister, Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, who said that nothing should be done that would disturb the ethnic and cultural balance of this nation, a statement as elusive as conscription if necessary, but not necessarily conscription. But it definitely had overtones of discrimination, and this was demonstrated in the attitude toward the Japanese Canadians during world war II, and similar episodes of that kind.
Can the hon. member inform the committee when the statement attributed to the late Mr. King was made, and his source?

The source of that statement was a speech made in the house by the then minister, Hon. Walter Harris, who referred to the policy of the department at that time and based it upon the policy statement

made by right hon. Mr. King. I haven't the quotation before me. It is in Hansard and I can get it for the hon. member and put it on the record if he so desires.
It was obvious that there was this element of discrimination. If my hon. friend from Carleton doubts that point I can refer to personal experiences that were mine during the early 1950's, with respect to Chinese immigration. Being particularly interested in the subject I concerned myself with many of the difficult Chinese cases which were particularly pertinent at the time, because of the Hong. Kong situation. For example, I could tell him of an instance-and this was the policy of the day as laid down in the regulations-where, because the only immigrants from Hong Kong who could enter were the unmarried children of Canadian Chinese, or their wives, a family tragedy occurred due to the inability of the married son of a Canadian Chinese family to enter Canada. He was the only member of the family, but notwithstanding many attempts to have the regulations changed he was declared inadmissible, which resulted in the suicide of his father. This typifies the lack of humanitarianism within the department but, as I suggested, there was a change in the mood and the spirit with regard to immigration matters, not only in Canada but in many other parts of the world.
It was part of the winds of change that resulted from the tragedy of world war II. It was a broad world wide wave of humanitarianism. It resulted from the emergence of new nations out of the holocaust of war. It resulted from the fact that the world had become a veritable whispering gallery and that we realized no man was an island. But nothing was done. I could go on and refer to the work of the United Nations, its educational and information work, and to such voluntary groups in Canada as the Canadian citizens council and the Canadian council of Christians and Jews, all of which helped to create an entirely new atmosphere of public opinion. However, the major breakthrough did not come until 1962. I want to pay tribute to Hon. Ellen Fairclough, who was the first lady in Canada to occupy ministerial responsibility and added a woman's humanitarian spirit to the discharge of her responsibilities in administering the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
A fundamental change occurred in the regulations in February, 1962, which did away once and for all with this element of discrimination based on racial considerations.
If, as the hon. member says, the former government did away with discrimination, why is it that Vancouver Canadian Chinese did not vote Conservative in 1962 and 1963?
Well, I am unfamiliar with the inner workings of the Liberal propaganda machine, but I know it is very effective in working on this new technique of hidden persuasion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Jealousy gets you nowhere.

I am not jealous at all because I am not interested in modern techniques of hidden persuasion, which have come under the careful scrutiny of responsible social scientists and have been found to be most dangerous to our free way of life. I am merely stating a fact, that the new regulations placed the whole problem of immigration on an entirely non-discriminatory basis, at least from a racial standpoint.
For example, it is now possible to admit anyone to Canada provided they have the skills and training required. The old criterion, disturbance of the ethnic and cultural balance, was definitely discriminatory. Now the criterion is skill and training, and it is also possible to bring in unsponsored immigrants on this basis. Formerly the only unsponsored immigrants who could come to Canada were those from countries within the very narrow category of the old commonwealth and western Europe. Those are the words that were used and they meant the non-coloured commonwealth countries. There are now no restrictions, and this has been evidenced by the recent increases in immigration from sources which were formerly rigidly restricted.
It is true that the regulations were changed, but that still does not resolve the problem because the success of the new regulations is dependant on how they are going to be administered. It is still possible to have discrimination through administration. I should like to know from the minister through his parliamentary secretary how many staff are provided in such places as Athens, the West Indies and Hong Kong, which are areas vitally interested in emigration to Canada and from which there is a comparatively small flow of immigrants at the present time. What kind of office space is provided for processing immigrants from these countries? If there is insufficient staff and inadequate office facilities you can exercise discrimination, of course, by administrative procedures.
Interim Supply
I was in Hong Kong a year ago and took it upon myself to visit our immigration office there.
You did not sign a wheat deal.

Someone has said I did not sign a wheat deal. There was no necessity to sign a wheat deal because that had already been done by my hon. friend, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, an act for which he was severely criticized by the Liberal opposition. Inasmuch as that topic has been introduced by the hon. member, may I say that I found Canadian prestige to be high in Hong Kong, because of the contacts that had been made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle who was then minister of agriculture.
I went to the immigration office there and I could readily understand why it required months to process applications. In fact, I worked for three years on an immigration case from Hong Kong.
Under your government.

I could understand why it took months, if not years, in order to process immigration cases from that country. The regulations have now cleared the way, but the regulations will mean nothing unless the administrative procedures are such as to facilitate the implementation of the regulations. The new minister was in Hong Kong a few months ago and he indicated that improvements were going to be made in this respect. I hope it will be possible either in the house, or in the committee that I trust will be set up, for him to give an outline of the improvements that have been made.
I could spend some time on the problems of citizenship and immigration but I do not want to delay the committee in this regard, other than to re-emphasize that there is now abroad in Canada and in the world the spirit of humanitarianism that was recognized by the former Conservative administration and which led to the then minister, Hon. Ellen Fair dough, bringing in enlightened regulations. I trust that the new administration will act in the same spirit that motivated her and the former government, the spirit that allowed a number of refugees to come to Canada from Hong Kong during a critical period there, the spirit which provided refuge in Canada for tuberculosis victims from the refugee camps of Europe and other parts of the world.
I think that Mr. T. G. McCormack, a businessman and the president of Dominion
Stores, reflected the attitude of the business

Interim Supply
community in regard to these matters when at the annual meeting of his company he suggested that Canada admit a million underprivileged refugees as a centennial project. This is the spirit that is abroad in the land and in the world and I hope it will not be stifled or stymied by the new administration. Like the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, who said he has read the speeches and press releases of the former minister and the new minister, I say that the speeches have been fine and have expressed exalted sentiments about the desirability of carrying on this process, but nowhere has there been any expression of a concrete policy and program.
Why was immigration so low in 1962?
I cannot hear the mumblings of the hon. member. If he wishes to ask a question I will be quite happy to listen to him.
I was wondering why immigration was so abnormally low in 1962?

Immigration has fluctuated from time to time in the history of Canada. I think the only explanation that can be given for that year which was prior to the introduction of the new regulations, is the discriminatory aspect of the former regulations which provided for immigrants from western Europe and the old commonwealth countries only, and these sources of immigrants were drying up because of the rising prosperity in Europe and the United Kingdom.
How about Canada in those days?
I think that is the only explanation for that.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Mr. Chairman, these hon. gentlemen-
I am only asking whether he will allow a question. He just has to say yes or no.

-on the government side are full of curiosity and questions. You would think I was the minister of immigration. I wish they would question their own minister instead of sitting back like trained seals and doing nothing.
I asked the hon. member if he would allow a question.
I have allowed many questions.

The hon. member was a minister in the former government and I believe he was a minister in March of 1959. Will he tell me why on March 19, 1959-I may have the date wrong-an order in council was passed by the former government in which Hon. Ellen Fairclough was minister of citizenship and immigration which refused admission to this county of sisters and brothers from any country except Great Britain and France, and then substituted the new regulations? Were these enlightened regulations which were passed in a spirit of humanitarianism? Would the hon. member tell me why this was done? It was only after a great uproar throughout the country that the order in council was rescinded by the then minister. I would appreciate it if the hon. member would tell me why that order in council was passed, when he was a minister of the government at that time.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is wrong on two counts. I was not a member of the government at that time.
I was not sure.
I did not become a member of the government until November of 1960 so I cannot answer for the order in council.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR LIMITATION OF ELECTION EXPENSES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-38, to amend the Canadian Elections Act (limiting election expenses).
He said: I do not wish to be deterred by any false modesty from saying that in my view if this bill were passed it would be one of the most important items in legislation which this house has dealt with, and I therefore invite the close attention of members of the house to this proposed legislation.
Bill No. C-38, to amend the Canada Elections Act, is designed to achieve its purpose by adding a new section to the act. This new section is designed to provide a reasonable and enforceable limitation on campaign expenses in federal elections. By the terms of the bill, permission to spend money in an election is restricted to two groups of people, the official agents of government candidates, and the parties. The restrictions as set out in the bill would allow the official agent to expend a maximum of 20 cents per elector on his roll. If we take constituencies of average size, containing 50,000 voters, this would mean that a limit of $10,000 would be imposed as far as the expenditure of a candidate is concerned. This, in my view, is surely enough-some people may think it is too much-to enable a candidate to conduct an adequate campaign.
Even more important, this bill proposes to limit the expenditure by parties to a maximum of 10 cents per elector in each constituency in which the party runs candidates. This would mean, if a party was running candidates in all the constituencies, an expenditure in the neighbourhood of $600,000. There is no restriction, of course, as to how the party may decide to spend the money, but there is provision for accountability and
[Mr. Favreau.}

the publication of details both as to the source and as to the expenditure of campaign funds.
The amount of $600,000 per party may seem like a lot of money but it is very much less than the two older parties, at least, are reputed to have spent in a number of elections in the past, and I suggest it is quite enough to permit the conduct of a campaign of moderate proportions to let the people of Canada know what the different parties stand for.
The bill provides for sworn statements setting out in detail the sources of election funds spent for political purposes, as well as the amounts disbursed by individual candidates or by agents. It also contains a clause, to which I invite the attention of hon. members, establishing the right of any person, corporate association or trade union to contribute to election campaigns, subject to the broad general limits contained in the bill.
It is my belief that this bill, or a similar bill, would mark a most important step forward in establishing a genuine democracy. The basic idea of democracy, as I understand it, is that the government is the servant of the people, that is, of all the people-the rich as well as the poor, the strong as well as the weak, the worker and the farmer as well as the businessman. Our system of regular elections and secret balloting is the machinery whereby we seek to preserve this relationship between government and people.
But it is my view that we have in Canada today only a half democracy or what might be called the caricature of a democracy, and one of the reasons for this situation is that in our election of representatives to parliament we do not give either the candidate or the electors a fair choice or a fair chance. We allow the scales to be weighted heavily in favour of candidates and parties who can secure large campaign funds. I suggest that if we were discussing a game we would not tolerate the fixing of the handicaps in a way which would ensure the victory of one side or the other by favouring those who could lay their hands on the most money. But we do this with respect to something far more important than any game, that is, in the choosing of the people who will be our representatives in parliament.
It seems to me that democracy today is threatened by the techniques of advertising saturation made possible by huge campaign funds. Individual leaders and parties are sold with the same banality as soap. In a recent election campaign I heard one party leader boast over the radio that money was no

problem in his campaign at all, and I do not think it is any coincidence that this same party leader-so we are informed, and, I think correctly-had his personality remade during the course of the election by public relations advisers who apparently found him not entirely satisfactory. In the course of the election they managed to modify his personality and create a public image which, it seems, did not correspond very much with the normal attributes of this particular individual. I do not know whether any members of the house have gathered the name of the man to whom I am referring; I would not wish to make any derogatory remarks about someone who has, since that election, occupied an important office.
But if we are to restore democracy today, against the threats of high-powered advertising campaigns financed by big money, we must limit campaign expenditures. We have been given a lead in this matter by the government of the province of Quebec which in 1963 enacted a statute limiting campaign funds. My bill-I will admit it frankly-is modelled upon the Quebec legislation in this field, though there are differences in detail. I think the Quebec legislature was a little too generous in the amount it allowed to be spent. Britain, which also has legislation limiting campaign funds, is far more modest in the amount it finds necessary to allow to enable the parties to put their cases before the electors. In my bill I have chosen a figure which lies somewhere between the two.
There are other reasons why this bill should be passed. I do not intend to give a historical account of the influence on governments of campaign funds from interested sources. This has been a feature of Canadian history, and I think he would be a bold man who would assert that such influence does not still exist, perhaps in a modified form. But whether it exists or not to any extent at the present time, I suggest it is clearly wrong and undemocratic that there should be undisclosed contributions made to parties for campaign purposes, usually I imagine without the extraction of any specific undertaking but nevertheless designed to secure a coincidence of view between the party and the people who make the contributions. I am putting this in delicate language but I think the facts of life are known to most members of the house.
There is another aspect to which I think we should pay attention at the present time. I am not a person who wrings his hands in alarm at the amount of American invest-
Canada Elections Act
ment in this country and the large extent of United States ownership of our business resources. I think if we have enough gumption in our own country to govern and manage our own affairs and direct our own investments intelligently the problem of American investment would not perhaps be as serious as some people think. I admit there are differences of opinion on this matter. But when we find that more than 50 per cent of our manufacturing industry-I think my figures are correct; it is certainly close to that-is owned by people who are not citizens of this country, and we have large, undisclosed campaign funds, I suggest that in order to prevent the possibility of the influence of those who are not citizens of this country on our political system, through the contribution of campaign funds, we should provide for a limitation, for one thing, and publicity as to the sources of these campaign funds for another.
I think the people of this country have the right to expect that those who are proud-they should be proud-to contribute to the parties they believe in, should have the courage to let their names and the facts be published in respect of these things. I know that goes against the grain and tradition of some people, perhaps, in this house, but I suggest it would be an important step in the direction of a real democracy. The steady influence of large campaign funds in my view distorts and destroys democracy.
This particular bill that I have put before the house I do not suggest for a minute is the last word on the subject. I think that if this bill were referred to the committee on privileges and elections, its details could be studied, it could be improved so as to make sure that the enforcement was adequate, and discussion could be had by members of the house as to whether the figures are right or wrong. But I do say, and I say as clearly as I can, that it would be a tremendous step forward if we would either pass this bill- and I am not quite that optimistic-or at least refer it to the committee on privileges and elections.
I say, particularly to hon. members opposite, with all their protestations about their concern for democracy and their progressive view, that these protestations will be tested by their attitude toward this particular bill. I would be very happy if they would say, "We have a better bill that we are prepared to promote ourselves". But unless they are prepared to do something like that, I say their protestations of progressive Liberalism mean nothing. If they are prepared to stick to the bad, old system of large, unsolicited,

Canada Elections Act
uncontrolled campaign funds and do nothing about it, then I say that the mask is off as far as I am concerned.
Mind you, Mr. Speaker, I do not think they will do that for a minute. As I look at hon. members opposite and know their concern about this matter, I feel sure they will accept this legislation and, if not accept it in total, at least not kill it by the familiar device, the disreputable device, I think, as far as members of this house are concerned, of talking it out because they are afraid to stand up and be counted on the issue of the bill.

speechtext:
Our system of government is one which we refer to frequently as a democratic representative government. The electorate in each constituency selects its representative, and each representative comes to the House of Commons to debate the questions of public policy confronting the country, and eventually, we hope, to decide those questions. The elected representatives are very important in our constitutional system, and consequently the election of those representatives is important. We do not have in this country plebiscitarian democracy; we have a representative system of government.
That brings me directly to the question of election expenses, for elections, as the hon. member for Greenwood has said, do cost a lot of money. Each serious candidate wants to get elected; otherwise, he would not be running. Each party wants to elect as 20220-397J
Canada Elections Act
many of its candidates as possible; otherwise, presumably, the party would not field its candidates. But what happens? Once an election begins-and it goes on a long time- rumours start to spread that such and such a candidate is spending a fabulous amount of money. Immediately his competitors feel obliged to do better. Parties try to outdo each other. And I suspect that newspapermen, radio and television station proprietors, and the like are not above implying quietly to candidates and parties that unless they are a little more forthcoming with their money their chances of convincing the electorate to support them are likely to be small. In other words, election expenses tend to escalate during elections, and parties and candidates tend to overspend their budgets.
Quite aside from the function of electing representatives to sit in the House of Commons, elections serve another purpose, as indicated by the hon. member for Greenwood. In our democracy we cannot rely on the newspapers, radio announcers and commentators, and television announcers and commentators alone to put the case to the electorate. The candidates and the parties themselves must take their case to the high court of the electorate. This means that when we talk of limiting campaign expenditures we must talk about it in a way consistent with the other function of elections. The candidates must have enough money committed to their use to put their case before the electorate through the available media. This is an essential part of our system of democratic representative government, and it costs money.
I hope all of us in this house would agree that the amount of money a man has, be he rich or poor, has no direct bearing on his ability to be a good member of this House of Commons. We realize that the older a man is, if he has been successful in his business or profession, the more money he is likely to have.
The situation is this. Competitions take place in which money is almost always a necessary requirement for electoral success; yet the amount of money a man has is largely irrelevant to his ability to contribute to the good government of the country.
We all know that most candidates receive contributions to their campaign funds. Unfortunately the notion seems to prevail that there is something extremely sordid about this. It is amusing to see how some of the academic enthusiasts of representative government turn righteous and sad when they

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to hear the remarks of the parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State (Mr. Stewart) when he says the government is now giving some very serious consideration to the problem of what might be called escalating, or at least, increasing election campaign funds. In my opinion the bill presented to us this afternoon by the hon. member for Greenwood is far from perfect in what the results of its application would bring about, but at the same time I think it is time the members of this house spent a few minutes discussing the problem that is raised by the introduction of this bill.
Canada Elections Act
First of all, the hon. member sets some limits in respect to the amount that each candidate or his official agent may spend within the boundaries of his constituency. I believe he has the amount of 20 cents per elector. I can understand that this is enforceable. I am sure that, regardless of where the funds come from, it is reasonable to assume that almost all of the money that would be spent by the candidate's official agent and his party organization would be confined within his constituency. So, while 20 cents may be too high, in my opinion it is more than adequate.
He goes on to provide in this bill:
In a general election the election expenses shall be limited as follows:
(a) by a party to a sum not exceeding in the aggregate (10c.) cents per elector in each electoral district in which such party has an official candidate;
I presume this clause applies to a national political party, but there is no provision in the bill showing how you will determine how much is spent within each constituency by a national party.
In almost all parts of Canada television signals transcend the boundaries of constituencies, for example in Vancouver, Regina and Lethbridge. I happen to know about Lethbridge because it is close to home, and so I will talk about it. The signal from the station in Lethbridge is beamed into three constituencies. It covers 25 per cent of the Medicine Hat constituency, all of the Lethbridge constituency and possibly half of the Macleod constituency. Are they going to take into consideration all these percentages when they allocate the amount that is effectively being spent within the boundaries of each of these constituencies?
There is another very important matter that must be considered when we are thinking of limiting the amount of money to be spent for advertising during an election campaign. I refer to C.B.C. free time broadcasting. We know that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, under some formula that they do not follow anyway, allocates free time to what they consider to be national political parties that meet the conditions of a formula they have laid down. They allocate a certain amount of free time on this basis. But the allocation of free time is just as important and, in fact, in many ways more important than the question of expense money because we know that during election campaigns, or at any time, I believe, the C.B.C. does not sell time on a network basis to any political party. Therefore if there is to be an effective

Canada Elections Act
distribution of this kind of advertising it certainly cannot be done by limiting the amount of money each party is allowed to spend.
This raises a number of problems. It raises the problem of what is a proper allocation of time. Should it be done on a national scale from Vancouver island to Newfoundland? Should the percentage of time allocated be on the basis of the popular vote that a particular party received in the immediately preceding election? Should we take into consideration the different levels of support for a political party in various regions? And so on.
These are things that must be considered when one is thinking of restricting the amount of advertising a party can do during an election campaign. I know that prior to the 1962 election the C.B.C. informed the Social Credit party they would not be allowed any free time during the campaign. We took issue with this decision. The only one of the five conditions they laid down that we could not meet had to do with having elected members in the House of Commons. It is well known that all of our members were defeated in 1958, but every other condition had been met by our party. We had nominated a sufficient number of candidates, we had candidates in three or more provinces and we had had a national convention and had elected a national leader. We met all the other conditions contained in the regulations.
It so happens, Mr. Speaker, that during election campaigns there are no members of parliament. Parliament is dissolved and so this regulation could not apply. There were no political parties during the election campaign which had any representation in the House of Commons because the house had been dissolved. Whether or not this was the argument that changed their mind I do not know, but we were allocated a small amount of free time on the national C.B.C. network.
I agree with what the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) said with regard to suspecting that large amounts of money are contributed to the campaign funds of certain political parties in the hope at least, whether or not strings are attached, that some action will be taken that will repay these people for the contributions they have made to these funds. I think the ideal situation would be for all the money a member wanted to spend to be collected within his own constituency. Then there would be no strings attached so far as anybody outside that constituency was

concerned and the member would only be responsible to the people he represented in the House of Commons. I am not suggesting I have a formula for setting up conditions that would lead to this ideal situation, but certainly I believe that members of the house should accurately represent the people who have elected them, with no strings attached to them by anyone beyond the border of their constituencies.
Much more could be said but there are only a few minutes left and I know that a number of members wish to speak on this subject. I believe that something should be done. No one in the house is so naive any more as to believe that the amount of money a candidate has at his disposal does not have a very direct influence on his chances of being elected. We know that good advertising requires the repetition of simple slogans in the newspapers and on television, and if a candidate is going to have a lot of repetition of his campaign slogans he has to have a lot of money to pay for this advertising. While I do not believe that the bill suggests solutions to all of the problems that members of the house know exist with regard to election campaigns, I think it is well that we have had some discussion of this subject.

There are other difficulties in connection with this bill which come to my mind, namely the definition of expenses. I should like to point out that in my own campaign, as well as the campaigns of other candidates in the Toronto area, volunteer workers made election signs, prepared material and this sort of thing. I do not know how you define these things. The time was donated, and so on. However, some candidates have to buy this election material and they would have to list these expenses. There is a difficulty here which would apply to a number of things. The hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart) said independent groups of citizens may buy television time or may donate election signs or printed material. This would be a difficulty that is not sufficiently covered in this bill.

It is my opinion-

speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member would permit me to ask him a question?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR LIMITATION OF ELECTION EXPENSES
speechtext: It is perhaps a sort of doublebarrelled question. The hon. member has raised certain difficulties relating to the details of the bill. Would he tell the house if he is in favour of the principle? If he is in favour of the principle, does he not think it would be proper to allow the committee to deal with the difficulties he raises, rather than to kill the bill by having someone talk it out?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR LIMITATION OF ELECTION EXPENSES
speechtext:
The hon. member asked me if I was in favour of the principle of the bill. I thought I made it clear at the outset of my remarks that I was in favour of the principle of the bill. I should like to consider myself as one of the strongest advocates for limiting campaign expenses. I should like also to support the argument which was made concerning some of the expenses being covered by the public treasury. I feel this is one of the most effective ways of equalizing the opportunities of candidates.
I believe that one of the things we must consider very soon in connection with this whole matter of campaign expenses concerns television time. I agree with the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) that this is a problem. I think it is a growing problem and if we do not turn our attention to it very soon, it is one that is going to get away from us. I should like to suggest that no one should be allowed to buy time on televison either from the C.B.C. or the private networks. I feel this time should be provided to political parties and candidates as a public service and as a condition of the granting of a television licence.
I feel this whole question of television time is becoming a much more important factor in elections than many of us would like to admit, or perhaps than many of us realize. I feel it is a matter to which we must turn our attention immediately. I strongly urge the government to amend the Broadcasting Act to cover this problem. I feel it is a big hurdle that we have to overcome before the next election. In my opinion, there is no reason why private television stations that are granted a franchise in a particular area should not make some time available to candidates and parties, just as the C.B.C. does, on a free basis.

Canada Elections Act
The hon. member lor Medicine Hat raised a question concerning the allocation of time. I suggest this is a difficulty and that it can be overcome by action by the appropriate body. The board of broadcast governors should be involved in the allocation of this time and the working out of a formula. I am not interested in just how that is going to be done. I do suggest this is an area which demands top priority. I know that during some of the election campaigns, particularly in Toronto, some of the candidates were on television practically all of the time. I must say it did not do them a lot of good in the last campaign. However, it is a factor and it will be a factor for a long time. It is one that we have to face.

I believe
it is clear from what has been stated by all hon. members, in fact by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) himself, that this is a thoroughly bad bill. Applying his own criteria, this is a bill which should not be passed by the house. The hon. member, in presenting the bill, has obviously failed to grapple with the basic problem of defining a political party. What is the type of entity that should be covered by the bill? I do not believe the hon. member is entitled to get up in this house and say, "I have not touched on the main question involved in this issue but I think the house should give this bill approval in principle". I do not believe the bill should be given approval in principle. I feel this house can, without any hesitation at all, refuse to proceed with what is essentially a very badly put together piece of legislation.
For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I should like to have permission to call it six o'clock.

speechtext: I should like to direct some questions to the acting house leader, whoever that may happen to be. There are three questions I should like to ask in order to assist the house in the conduct of the business next week. May I ask this, as question No. 1: Will the government, in response to the many requests made from this side of the house, refer three or four departments of estimates to special or standing committees? My second question is this: Will the government give an undertaking to the house that for the remainder of this session at least two full days a week will be set aside for a discussion of the main estimates, as has been the practice in other sessions? My third question is: If neither of these plans is followed, will the government let us know when during this session the main estimates are to be considered and how much time will be made available for that purpose?

Mr. Speaker, in reply to the questions raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, first of all as to the referral of departmental estimates to standing committees, I may say that I could not undertake this without consultation with the ministers involved in the particular departments. However, I will indicate to him that I will take the matter up with the ministers involved.
The second question really deals with the order of business for the remainder of this portion of the session.
